1
任城王雲，年五歲，恭宗崩，號哭不絕聲。 世祖聞之而呼，抱之泣曰：「汝何知而有成人之意也！」 和平五年封，拜使持節、侍中、征東大將軍、和龍鎮都大將。 顯祖時，拜都督中外諸軍事、中都坐大官，聽理民訟，甚收時譽。 延興中，顯祖集羣僚，欲禪位於京兆王子推。 王公卿士，莫敢先言。 雲進曰：「陛下方隆太平，臨覆四海，豈得上違宗廟，下棄兆民。 父子相傳，其來久矣，皇魏之興，未之有革。 皇儲正統，聖德夙章。 陛下必欲割捐塵務，頤神清曠者，冢副之寄，宜紹寶曆，若欲捨儲，輕移宸極，恐非先聖之意，駭動人情。 又，天下是祖宗之天下，而陛下輒改神器，上乖七廟七靈，下長姦亂之道，此是禍福所由，願深思慎之。」 太尉源賀又進曰：「陛下今欲外選諸王而禪位于皇叔者，臣恐春秋蒸嘗，昭穆有亂，脫萬世之後，必有逆饗之譏，深願思任城之言。」 東陽公元丕等進曰：「皇太子雖聖德夙彰，然實沖幼。 陛下富於春秋，始覽機政，普天景仰，率土傒心，欲隆獨善，不以萬物為意，其若宗廟何，其若億兆何！」 顯祖曰：「儲宮正統，受終文祖，羣公相之，有何不可。」 於是傳位於高祖。 後蠕蠕犯塞，雲為中軍大都督，從顯祖討之，遇於大磧。 事具蠕蠕傳。 後仇池氐反，以雲為征西大將軍討平之。 除都督徐兗二州緣淮諸軍事、征東大將軍、開府、徐州刺史。 雲以太妃蓋氏薨，表求解任，顯祖不許，雲悲號動疾，乃許之。 性善撫綏，得徐方之心，為百姓所追戀。 送遺錢貨，一無所受。 顯祖聞而嘉之。 復拜侍中、中都大官，賜帛千匹、羊千口。 出為冀州刺史，仍本將軍。 雲留心政事，甚得下情，於是合州請戶輸絹五尺、粟五升以報雲恩。 高祖嘉之，遷使持節、都督陝西諸軍事、征南大將軍、長安鎮都大將、雍州刺史。 雲廉謹自修，留心庶獄，挫抑豪強，羣盜息止，州民頌之者千有餘人。 文明太后嘉之，賜帛千匹。 太和五年，薨於州。 遺令薄葬，勿受賵禭。 諸子奉遵其旨。 喪至京師，車駕親臨，哭之哀慟，贈以本官，諡曰康。 陪葬雲中之金陵。 雲長子澄，字道鎮，少而好學。 及康王薨，澄居喪以孝聞。 襲封，加征北大將軍。 高祖時，蠕蠕犯塞，加澄使持節、都督北討諸軍事以討之。 蠕蠕遁走，又以氐羌反叛，除都督梁益荊三州諸軍事、征南大將軍、梁州刺史。 文明太后引見澄，誡厲之，顧謂中書令李沖曰：「此兒風神吐發，德音閑婉，當為宗室領袖。 是行使之必稱我意。 卿但記之，我不妄談人物也。」 梁州氐帥楊仲顯、婆羅、楊卜兄弟及符叱盤等，自以居邊地險，世為山狡。 澄至州，量彼風俗，誘導懷附。 表送婆羅，授仲顯循城鎮副將，楊卜廣業太守，叱盤固道鎮副將，自餘首帥，各隨才而用之，款附者賞，違命加誅，於是仇池帖然，西南款順。 加侍中，賜衣一襲、乘馬一匹，以旌其能。 後轉征東大將軍、開府、徐州刺史，甚有聲績。 朝於京師，引見於皇信堂。 高祖詔澄曰：「昔鄭子產鑄刑書，而晉叔向非之。 此二人皆是賢士，得失竟誰？」 對曰：「鄭國寡弱，攝於強鄰，民情去就，非刑莫制，故鑄刑書以示威。 雖乖古式，合今權道，隨時濟世，子產為得。 而叔向譏議，示不忘古，可與論道，未可語權。」 高祖曰：「任城當欲為魏之子產也。」 澄曰：「子產道合當時，聲流竹素。 臣既庸近，何敢庶幾。 今陛下以四海為家，宣文德以懷天下，但江外尚阻，車書未一，季世之民，易以威伏，難以禮治。 愚謂子產之法，猶應暫用，大同之後，便以道化之。」 高祖心方革變，深善其對，笑曰：「非任城無以識變化之體。 朕方創改朝制，當與任城共萬世之功耳。」 後徵為中書令，改授尚書令。 蕭賾使庾蓽來朝，蓽見澄音韻遒雅，風儀秀逸，謂主客郎張彝曰：「往魏任城以武著稱，今魏任城乃以文見美也。」 時詔延四廟之子，下逮玄孫之冑，申宗宴於皇信堂，不以爵秩為列，悉序昭穆為次，用家人之禮。 高祖曰：「行禮已畢，欲令宗室各言其志，可率賦詩。」 特令澄為七言連韻，與高祖往復賭賽，遂至極歡，際夜乃罷。 後高祖外示南討，意在謀遷，齋於明堂左个，詔太常卿王諶，親令龜卜，易筮南伐之事，其兆遇革。 高祖曰：「此是湯武革命，順天應人之卦也。」 羣臣莫敢言。 澄進曰：「易言革者更也。 將欲應天順人，革君臣之命，湯武得之為吉。 階下帝有天下，重光累葉。 今曰卜征，乃可伐叛，不得云革命。 此非君人之卦，未可全為吉也。」 高祖厲聲曰：「象云『大人虎變』，何言不吉也！」 澄曰：「陛下龍興既久，豈可方同虎變！」 高祖勃然作色曰：「社稷我社稷，任城而欲沮眾也！」 澄曰：「社稷誠知陛下之社稷，然臣是社稷之臣子，豫參顧問，敢盡愚衷。」 高祖既銳意必行，惡澄此對，久之乃解，曰：「各言其志，亦復何傷。」 車駕還宮，便召澄，未及昇階，遙謂曰：「向者之革卦，今更欲論之。 明堂之忿，懼眾人競言，阻我大計，故厲色怖文武耳，想解朕意也。」 乃獨謂澄曰：「今日之行，誠知不易。 但國家興自北土，徙居平城，雖富有四海，文軌未一，此間用武之地，非可文治，移風易俗，信為甚難。 崤函帝宅，河洛王里，因茲大舉，光宅中原，任城意以為何如？」 澄曰：「伊洛中區，均天下所據，陛下制御華夏，輯平九服，蒼生聞此，應當大慶。」 高祖曰：「北人戀本，忽聞將移，不能不驚擾也。」 澄曰：「此既非常之事，當非常人所知，唯須決之聖懷，此輩亦何能為也。」 高祖曰：「任城便是我之子房。」 加撫軍大將軍、太子少保，又兼尚書左僕射。 及駕幸洛陽，定遷都之策，高祖詔曰：「遷移之旨，必須訪眾。 當遣任城馳驛向代，問彼百司，論擇可否。 近日論革，今真所謂革也，王其勉之。」 既至代都，眾聞遷詔，莫不驚駭。 澄援引今古，徐以曉之，眾乃開伏。 澄遂南馳還報，會車駕於滑臺。 高祖大悅曰：「若非任城，朕事業不得就也。」 從幸鄴宮，除吏部尚書。 及幸代，車駕北巡，留澄銓簡舊臣。 初，魏自公侯以下，迄于選臣，動有萬數，冗散無事。 澄品為三等，量其優劣，盡其能否之用，咸無怨者。 駕還洛京，復兼右僕射。 高祖至北邙，遂幸洪池，命澄侍昇龍舟，因賦詩以序懷。 高祖曰：「朕昨夜夢一老公，頭鬢皓白，正理冠服，拜立路左。 朕怪而問之，自云晉侍中嵇紹，故此奉迎。 神爽卑懼，似有求焉。」 澄對曰：「晉世之亂，嵇紹以身衞主，殞命御側，亦是晉之忠臣； 比干遭紂兇虐，忠諫剖心，可謂殷之良士。 二人俱死於王事，墳塋並在於道周。 然陛下徙御經殷墟而弔比干，至洛陽而遺嵇紹，當是希恩而感夢。」 高祖曰：「朕何德，能幽感達士也。 然實思追禮先賢，標揚忠懿，比干、嵇紹皆是古之誠烈，而朕務濃於比干，禮略於嵇紹，情有愧然。 既有此夢，或如任城所言。」 於是求其兆域，遣使弔祭焉。 蕭鸞既殺蕭昭業而自立，昭業雍州刺史曹虎請以襄陽內附。 分遣諸將，車駕將自赴之。 豫州又表，虎奉誠之使不復重來。 高祖引澄及咸陽王禧、彭城王勰、司徒馮誕、司空穆亮、鎮南李沖等議之。 高祖曰：「比得邊州表云，襄陽慕化，朕將鳴鑾江沔，為彼聲勢。 今復表稱，更無後信，於行留之計，竟欲如何？」 禧等或云宜行，或言宜止。 高祖曰：「眾人紛紜，意見不等，朕莫知所從。 必欲盡行留之勢，使言理俱暢者，宜有客主，共相起發。 任城與鎮南為應留之議，朕當為宜行之論，諸公俱坐聽得失，長者從之。」 於是高祖曰：「二賢試言留計也。」 沖對曰：「臣等正以徒御草創，人斯樂安，內而應者未審，不宜輕爾動發。」 高祖曰：「襄陽款問，似當是虛。 亦知初遷之民，無宜勞役。 脫歸誠有實，即當乘其悅附，遠則有會稽之會，近則略平江北。 如其送款是虛，且可遊巡淮楚，問民之瘼，使彼土蒼生，知君德之所在，復何所損而惜此一舉？ 脫降問是實，而停不撫接，不亦稽阻款誠，毀朕大略也。」 澄曰：「降問若審，應有表質。 而使人一返，靜無音問，其詐也可見。 今代遷之眾，人懷戀本，細累相攜，始就洛邑，居無一椽之室，家闕儋石之糧，而使怨苦即戎，泣當白刃，恐非歌舞之師也。 今茲區宇初構，又東作方興，正是子來百堵之日，農夫肆力之秋，宜寬彼逋誅，惠此民庶。 且三軍已援，無稽赴接。 苟其款實，力足納撫，待克平襄沔，然後動駕。 今無故勞涉，空為往返，恐挫損天威，更成賊膽，願上覽盤庚始遷之艱難，下矜詩人由庚之至詠，輯寧新邑，惠康億兆。」 而司空亮以為宜行，公卿皆同之。 澄謂亮曰：「公在外見旌鉞既張，而有憂色，每聞談論，不願此行，何得對聖顏更如斯之語也。 面背不同，事涉欺佞，非所謂論道之德，更失國士之體，或有傾側，當由公輩佞臣。」 李沖曰：「任城王可謂忠於社稷，願陛下深察其言。 臣等在外，皆憚征行，唯貴與賤，不謀同辭，仰願聖心裁其可否。」 高祖曰：「任城適以公等從朕，有如此論。 不從朕者，何必皆忠而通識安危也。 小忠是大忠之賊，無乃似諸？」 澄曰：「臣既愚闇，不識大理，所可言者，雖涉小忠，要是竭盡微款，不知大忠者竟何據？」 高祖曰：「任城脫居台鼎之任，欲令大忠在己也。」 澄曰：「臣誠才非台弼，智闕和鼎，脫得濫居公鉉，庶當官而行，不負愚志。」 高祖大笑。 澄又謂亮曰：「昔汲黯於漢武前面折公孫食脫粟飯，臥布被，云其詐也。 于時公孫謙讓下之。 武帝歎汲黯至忠，公孫長者，二人稱賢。 公既道均昔士，願思長者之言。」 高祖笑曰：「任城欲自比汲黯也。 且所言是公，未知得失所在，何便謝司空也。」 駕遂南伐。 五等開建，食邑一千戶。 後從征至懸瓠，以篤疾還京。 駕餞之汝濆，賦詩而別。 車駕還洛，引見王公侍臣於清徽堂。 高祖曰：「此堂成來，未與王公行宴樂之禮。 後東閤廡堂粗復始就，故今與諸賢欲無高而不昇，無小而不入。」 因之流化渠。 高祖曰：「此曲水者亦有其義，取乾道曲成，萬物無滯。」 次之洗煩池。 高祖曰：「此池中亦有嘉魚。」 澄曰：「此所謂『魚在在藻，有頒其首』。」 高祖曰：「且取『王在靈沼，於牣魚躍』。」 次之觀德殿。 高祖曰：「射以觀德，故遂命之。」 次之凝閑堂。 高祖曰：「名目要有其義，此蓋取夫子閑居之義。 不可縱奢以忘儉，自安以忘危，故此堂後作茅茨堂。」 謂李沖曰：「此東曰步元廡，西曰遊凱廡。 此堂雖無唐堯之君，卿等當無愧於元、凱。」 沖對曰：「臣既遭唐堯之君，不敢辭元、凱之譽。」 高祖曰：「光景垂落，朕同宗則有載考之義，卿等將出無遠，何得默爾，不示德音。」 即命黃門侍郎崔光、郭祚，通直郎邢巒、崔休等賦詩言志。 燭至，公卿辭退。 李沖再拜上千萬歲壽。 高祖曰：「卿向以燭至致辭，復獻千萬之壽，朕報卿以南山之詩。」 高祖曰：「燭至辭退，庶姓之禮； 在夜載考，宗族之義。 卿等且還，朕與諸王宗室，欲成此夜飲。」 又從幸鄴。 還洛，以出納之勞，增邑五百戶。 坐公事免官。 尋兼吏部尚書。 恒州刺史穆泰在州謀反，推朔州刺史陽平王頤為主。 頤表其狀。 高祖召澄入見凝閑堂，曰：「適得陽平表曰，穆泰謀為不軌，招誘宗室。 脫或必然，遷京甫爾，北人戀舊，南北紛擾，朕洛陽不立也。 此事非任城不辦，可為我力疾向北。 如其弱也，直往擒翦； 若其勢強，可承制發并肆兵以殄之。 雖知王患，既是國家大事，不容辭也。」 澄曰：「泰等愚惑，正戀本為此，非有遠圖。 臣誠怯弱，不憚是輩，雖復患惙，豈敢有辭。 謹當罄盡心力，繼之以死，願陛下勿憂。」 高祖笑曰：「得任城此行，朕復何憂也。」 遂授節，銅虎、竹使符，御仗，左右，仍行恒州事。 行達雁門，太守夜告泰已握眾西就陽平，城下聚結，唯見弓仗。 澄聞便速進。 時右丞孟斌曰：「事不可量，須依敕召并肆兵，然後徐動。」 澄曰：「泰既構逆，應據堅城，而更迎陽平，度其所為，似當勢弱。 泰既不相拒，無故發兵，非宜也。 但速往鎮之，民心自定。」 遂倍道兼行，出其不意。 又遣治書侍御史李煥先赴，至即擒泰，民情怡然。 窮其黨與，罪人皆得，鉅鹿公陸叡、安樂侯元隆等百餘人皆獄禁。 具狀表聞，高祖覽表大悅，召集公卿以下以表示之，曰：「我任城可謂社稷臣也，尋其罪案，正復臯陶斷獄，豈能過之。」 顧謂咸陽王等曰：「汝等脫當其處，不能辦此。」 車駕尋幸平城，勞澄曰：「任城此行，深副遠寄。」 對曰：「陛下威靈遠被，罪人無所逃刑，臣何勞之有。」 引見逆徒，無一人稱枉，時人莫不歎之。 高祖顧謂左右曰：「昔仲尼云：『聽訟吾猶人也，必也使無訟乎。』 然聖人之聽訟，殆非常人所匹，必也無訟，今日見之矣。」 以澄正尚書。 車駕南伐，留澄居守，復兼右僕射。 澄表請以國秩一歲租布帛助供軍資，詔受其半。 高祖幸鄴，值高車樹者反叛，車駕將親討之。 澄表諫不宜親行。 會江陽王繼平之，乃止。 高祖還洛，引見公卿。 高祖曰：「營國之本，禮教為先。 朕離京邑以來，禮教為日新以不？」 澄對曰：「臣謂日新。」 高祖曰：「朕昨入城，見車上婦人冠帽而著小襦襖者，若為如此，尚書何為不察？」 澄曰：「著猶少於不著者。」 高祖曰：「深可怪也！ 任城意欲令全著乎？ 一言可以喪邦者，斯之謂歟？ 可命史官書之。」 又曰：「王者不降佐於蒼昊，皆拔才而用之。 朕失於舉人，任許一羣婦人輩奇事，當更銓簡耳。 任城在省，為舉天下綱維，為當署事而已？」 澄曰：「臣實署事而已。」 高祖曰：「如此便一令史足矣，何待任城。」 又曰：「我遣舍人宣詔，何為使小人聞之？」 澄曰：「時雖有幹吏，去榜亦遠。」 高祖曰：「遠則不聞，聞則不遠。 既得聞詔，理故可知。」 於是留守羣臣遂免冠謝罪。 尋除尚書右僕射。 蕭寶卷遣其太尉陳顯達入寇漢陽。 是時高祖不豫，引澄入見清徽堂。 詔曰：「顯達侵亂，沔陽不安，朕不親行，莫攘此賊。 朕疾患淹年，氣力惙弊，如有非常，委任城大事。 是段任城必須從朕。」 澄涕泣對曰：「臣謹當竭股肱之力，以命上報。」 遂從駕南伐。 高祖崩，澄受顧命。 世宗初，有降人嚴叔懋告尚書令王肅遣孔思達潛通寶卷，圖為叛逆，寶卷遣俞公喜送敕於肅，公喜還南，肅與裴叔業馬為信。 澄信之，乃表肅將叛，輒下禁止。 咸陽、北海二王奏澄擅禁宰輔，免官歸第。 尋出為平西將軍、梁州刺史。 辭以母老。 除安東將軍、相州刺史，復固辭。 改授安西將軍、雍州刺史。 尋徵赴季秋講武。 除都督淮南諸軍事、鎮南大將軍、開府、揚州刺史。 下車封孫叔敖之墓，毀蔣子文之廟。 頻表南伐，世宗不許。 又辭母老，乞解州任，寢而不報。 加散騎常侍。 澄表曰：「臣參訓先朝，藉規有日，前言舊軌，頗亦聞之。 又昔在恒代，親習皇宗，熟祕序疑庭無闕日。 臣每於侍坐，先帝未嘗不以書典在懷，禮經為事，周旋之則，不輟於時。 自鳳舉中京，方隆禮教，宗室之範，每蒙委及，四門之選，負荷銓量。 自先皇升遐，未遑修述，學宮虛荷四門之名，宗人有闕四時之業，青衿之緒，於茲將廢。 臣每惟其事，竊所傷懷。 伏惟聖略宏遠，四方罕務，宴安之辰，於是乎在。 何為太平之世，而令子衿之歎興焉； 聖明之日，而使宗人之訓闕焉。 愚謂可敕有司，修復皇宗之學，開闢四門之教，使將落之族，日就月將。」 詔曰：「冑子崇業，自古盛典，國均之訓，無應久廢，尚書更可量宜修立。」 澄又表母疾解州任，不聽。 蕭衍將張囂之寇陷夷陵戍，澄遣輔國將軍成興步騎赴討，大破之，復夷陵，囂之遁走。 又遣長風戍主奇道顯攻蕭衍陰山戍，破之，斬其戍主龍驤將軍、都亭侯梅興祖。 仍引攻白槀戍，又破之，斬其寧朔將軍、關內侯吳道爽。 澄表曰：「蕭衍頻斷東關，欲令巢湖汎溢。 湖周回四百餘里，東關合江之際，廣不過數十步，若賊計得成，大湖傾注者，則淮南諸戍必同晉陽之事矣。 又吳楚便水，且灌且掠，淮南之地，將非國有。 壽陽去江五百餘里，眾庶惶惶，並懼水害。 脫乘民之願，攻敵之虛，豫勒諸州，纂集士馬，首秋大集，則南瀆可為飲馬之津，霍嶺必成徙倚之觀，事貴應機，經略須早。 縱混一不可必果，江西自是無虞。 若猶豫緩圖，不加除討，關塞既成，襄陵方及，平原民戍定為魚矣。」 詔發冀、定、瀛、相、并、濟六州二萬人，馬一千五百匹，令仲秋之中畢會淮南，并壽陽先兵三萬，委澄經略。 先是朝議有南伐之意，以蕭寶夤為東揚州刺史據東城，陳伯之為江州刺史戍陽石，以澄總督二鎮，授之節度。 至是勒兵進討。 以東關水衝，大峴險要，東關縱水，陽石、合肥有急懸之切，不圖大峴，則歷陽有乘險之援，淮陵陸道，九山水路，並宜經略。 於是遣統軍傅豎眼、王神念等進次大峴、東關、九山、淮陵，皆分部諸將，倍道據之，總勒大眾，絡繹相接。 而神念克其關要、潁川二城，斬衍軍主費尼。 而寧朔將軍韋惠、龍驤將軍李伯由仍固大峴。 澄遣統軍党法宗、傅豎眼等進軍克之，遂圍白塔、牽城，數日之間，便即逃潰。 衍清溪戍望風散走。 衍徐州刺史司馬明素率眾三千，欲援九山； 徐州長史潘伯隣規固淮陵； 寧朔將軍王燮負險焦城。 法宗進克焦城，破淮陵，擒明素，斬伯隣。 其濟陰太守王厚強、廬江太守裴邃即亦奔退。 詔澄曰：「將軍文德內昭，武功外暢，奮揚大略，將蕩江吳。 長旌始舒，賊徒懾氣，銳旅方馳，東關席卷。 想江湖弭波，在旦夕耳。 所送首虜，並已聞之。」 初，澄出討之後，衍將姜慶真襲據壽春外郭，齊王蕭寶夤擊走之。 長史韋纘坐免官，澄以在外無坐。 遂攻鍾離。 又詔：「鍾離若食盡，三月已前，固有可克，如至四月，淮水泛長，舟行無礙，宜善量之。 前事捷也，此實將軍經略，勳有常焉。 如或以水盛難圖，亦可為萬全之計，不宜昧利無成，以貽後悔也。」 蕭衍冠軍將軍張惠紹，游擊將軍殷暹、驍騎將軍趙景悅、龍驤將軍張景仁等率眾五千，送糧鍾離。 澄遣統軍王足、劉思祖等邀擊惠紹等，大破之。 獲惠紹、殷暹、景仁及其屯騎校尉史文淵等軍主以上二十七人。 既而遇雨，淮水暴長，引歸壽春。 還既狼狽，失兵四千餘人。 頻表解州，世宗不許。 有司奏軍還失路，奪其開府，又降三階。 時蕭衍有移，求換張惠紹。 澄表請不許，詔付八座會議。 尚書令、廣陽王嘉等奏宜還之，詔乃聽還。 後果復寇邊。 轉澄鎮北大將軍、定州刺史。 初，民中每有橫調，百姓煩苦，前後牧守，未能蠲除，澄多所省減，民以忻賴。 又明黜陟賞罰之法，表減公園之地，以給無業貧口，禁造布絹不任衣者。 母孟太妃薨，居喪毀瘠，當世稱之。 服闋，除太子太保。 於時高肇當朝，猜忌賢戚。 澄為肇間構，常恐不全，乃終日昏飲，以示荒敗。 所作詭越，時謂為狂。 世宗夜崩，時事倉卒，高肇擁兵於外，肅宗沖幼，朝野不安。 澄疏斥不預機要，而朝望所屬，領軍于忠、侍中崔光等奏澄為尚書令，於是眾心忻服。 又加散騎常侍、驃騎大將軍，尋遷司空，加侍中，俄詔領尚書令。 初，正始之末，詔百司普昇一級，而執事者不達旨意，刺史、守、令限而不及。 澄奏曰：「竊惟雲構鬱起，澤及百司，企春望榮，內外同慶。 至於賞陟，不及守宰，爾來十年，冤訟不絕。 封回自鎮遠、安州入為太尉長史，元匡自征虜、恒州入作宗卿，二人遷授，並在先詔。 應蒙之理，備在於斯。 兼州佐停私之徒，陪臣郡丞之例，尚蒙天澤下降，榮及當時。 然參佐之來，皆因府主，今府主不霑，佐官獨預，棄本賞末，愚謂未允。 今計刺史、守、宰之官，請準回匡，悉同汎限，上允初旨百司之章，下覆訟者元元之心。」 詔曰：「自今已後，內外之事，嘗經先朝者，不得重聞。」 澄奏曰：「臣聞堯懸諫諍之鼓，舜置誹謗之木，皆所以廣耳目於芻蕘，達四聰於天下。 伏惟太祖開基，化隆自遠，累聖相承，於今九帝。 重光疊照，汚隆必同，與奪隨時，道無恒體。 思過如渴，言重千金，故稱無諱之朝，邁蹤三、五。 高祖沖年纂曆，文明協統，變官易律，未為違典。 及慈聖臨朝，母儀宇縣，爰發慈令，垂心滯獄，深枉者仰日月於九泉，微屈者希曲照於盆下。 今乃格以先朝，限以一例，斯誠奉遵之本心，實乖元元之至望。 在于謙挹，有乖舊典。 謹尋抱枉求直，或經累朝。 毫釐之差，正之宜速； 謬若千里，駟馬弗追。 故禮有損益，事有可否，父有諍子，君有諫臣，琴瑟不調，理宜改作。 是以防川之論，小決則通； 鄉校之言，擁則敗國。 矧伊陳屈，而可抑以先朝。 且先朝屈者，非故屈之，或有司愛憎，或執事濁僻，空文致法，以誤視聽。 如此冤塞，彌在可哀。 僭之與濫，寧失不經，乞收今旨，還依前詔。」 詔曰：「省奏，深體毗贊之情，三皇異軌，五代殊風，一時之制，何必詮改。 必謂虛文設旨，理在可申者，何容不同來執。 可依往制。」 澄表上皇誥宗制并訓詁各一卷，意欲皇太后覽之，思勸戒之益。 又奏利國濟民所宜振舉者十條。 一曰律度量衡，公私不同，所宜一之。 二曰宜興學校，以明黜陟之法。 三曰宜興滅繼絕，各舉所知。 四曰五調之外，一不煩民，任民之力，不過三日。 五曰臨民之官，皆須黜陟，以旌賞罰。 六曰逃亡代輸，去來年久者，若非伎作，任聽即住。 七曰邊兵逃走，或實陷沒，皆須精檢； 三長及近親，若實隱之，徵其代輸，不隱勿論。 八曰工商世業之戶，復徵租調，無以堪濟，今請免之，使專其業。 九曰三長禁姦，不得隔越相領，戶不滿者，隨近并合。 十曰羽林虎賁，邊方有事，暫可赴戰，常戍宜遣蕃兵代之。 靈太后下其奏，百僚議之，事有同否。 時四中郎將兵數寡弱，不足以襟帶京師，澄奏宜以東中帶滎陽郡，南中帶魯陽郡，西中帶恒農郡，北中帶河內郡，選二品、三品親賢兼稱者居之，省非急之作，配以強兵，如此則深根固本、強幹弱枝之義也。 靈太后初將從之，後議者不同，乃止。 澄又重奏曰：「固本宜強，防微在豫，故雖有文事，不忘武功。 況今南蠻仍獷，北妖頻結，來事難圖，勢同往變。 脫暴勃忽起，振動關畿，四府羸卒，何以防擬。 平康之世，可以寄安，遺之久長，恐非善策。 如臣愚見，郎將領兵，兼總民職，省官實祿，於是乎在。 求還依前增兵益號，將位既重，則念報亦深，軍郡相依，則表裏俱濟，朝廷無四顧之憂，姦宄絕窺覦之望矣。」 卒不納。 又以流人初至遠鎮，衣食無資，多有死者，奏并其妻子給糧一歲，從之。 尋以疾患，求解任，不許。 蕭衍於浮山斷淮為堰，以灌壽春，乃除使持節、大將軍、大都督、南討諸軍事，勒眾十萬，將出彭宋，尋淮堰自壞，不行。 澄以北邊鎮將選舉彌輕，恐賊虜闚邊，山陵危迫，奏求重鎮將之選，修警備之嚴，詔不從。 賊虜入寇，至於舊都，鎮將多非其人，所在叛亂，犯逼山陵，如澄所慮。 澄奏都城府寺猶未周悉，今軍旅初寧，無宜發眾，請取諸職人及司州郡縣犯十杖已上百鞭已下收贖之物，絹一匹，輸磚二百，以漸修造。 詔從之。 太傅、清河王懌表奏其事，遂寢不行。 澄又奏曰：「臣聞賞必以道，用防淫人之姦； 罰不濫及，以戒良士之困。 刑者，侀也。 每垂三宥，秉律執請，不得已而用之。 是故小大之獄，察之以情，一人呼嗟，或虧王道。 刑罰得失，乃興廢之所由也。 竊聞司州牧、高陽王臣雍栲殺奉朝請韓元昭、前門下錄事姚敬賢，雖因公事，理實未盡。 何者？ 太平之世，草不橫伐，行葦之感，事驗隆周。 若昭等狀彰，死罪以定，應刑於都市，與眾棄之； 如其疑似不分，情理未究，不宜以三清九流之官杖下便死，輕絕民命，傷理敗法。 往年州於大市鞭殺五人，及檢贓狀，全無寸尺。 今復酷害，一至於此。 朝野云云，咸懷驚愕。 若殺生在下，虐專於臣，人君之權，安所復用。 自開古以來，明明之世，未聞斯比也。 武王曰：『吾不以一人之命而易天下。』 蓋重民命也。 請以見事付廷尉推究，驗其為劫之狀，察其栲殺之理，使是非分明，幽魂獲雪。」 詔從之。 澄當官而行，無所回避。 又奏墾田授受之制八條，甚有綱貫，大便於時。 前來尚書文簿，諸曹須，則出借。 時公車署以理冤事重。 奏請真案。 澄執奏以尚書政本，特宜遠慎，故凡所奏事，閣道通之，蓋以祕要之切，防其宣露，寧有古制所重，今反輕之，內猶設禁，外更寬也。 宜繕寫事意，以付公車。
Yun, Prince of Rencheng, was only five when Gongzong died, yet he wailed without stopping. Shizu heard and called for him, took him in his arms, and wept. "How is it that you already have a grown man's heart?" In Heping year 5 he received his fief and was made Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, Grand General Who Conquers the East, and commander of Helong Garrison. Under Xianzu he commanded the armies inside and outside the court, served as seated high minister of the central capital, heard civil suits, and won wide renown. During the Yanxing era, Xianzu gathered his ministers, intending to abdicate to Zitui, Prince of Jingzhao. Among the princes, dukes, ministers, and officers, no one dared speak first. Yun stepped forward. "Your Majesty is raising an age of peace and shelters all within the four seas. How could you turn away from the ancestral temples above and cast off the people below? Father-to-son succession has long been the rule; since imperial Wei arose, it has never been altered. The crown prince is the rightful heir, and his virtue has shone since early youth. If Your Majesty truly wishes to lay aside worldly affairs and nourish your spirit in quiet freedom, the throne should pass to the heir. If you set the heir aside and lightly move the imperial pivot, I fear this defies the former sages and will shock the hearts of men. Moreover, the realm belongs to the ancestors. If Your Majesty suddenly changes the sacred vessel, you will offend the ancestral spirits above and open the way to treachery and disorder below. Fortune and disaster begin here; please think deeply and proceed with care." Grand Marshal Yuan He also spoke. "If Your Majesty chooses from among the princes and abdicates to an imperial uncle, I fear the order of the ancestral rites will be thrown into confusion, and later ages will condemn the offerings as improper. I beg you to weigh Rencheng's words." Duke Yuan Pi of Dongyang and the others added, "Although the crown prince's virtue is already clear, he is still very young. Your Majesty is young and has only begun to govern; all under heaven look to you, and every land waits on your heart. If you prize private purity and give no thought to the world, what becomes of the ancestral temples? What becomes of the people?" Xianzu replied, "The crown prince is the rightful line, receiving the succession from Wenzu. With all of you to assist him, what could be wrong?" Thereupon he passed the throne to Gaozu. Later, when the Rouran raided the frontier, Yun served as grand commander of the central army and followed Xianzu against them, meeting them in the great desert. The affair is recorded in the Rouran biography. Later, when the Qiuchi Di rebelled, Yun was made Grand General Who Conquers the West and put them down. He was appointed commander of military affairs along the Huai in Xu and Yan provinces, Grand General Who Conquers the East, opened his office, and served as inspector of Xu Province. When Yun's grand consort, Lady Gai, died, he asked to resign. Xianzu refused, but Yun grieved and wailed until he fell ill, and only then was he allowed to step down. He was naturally good at soothing and governing people, won the hearts of Xu, and was remembered fondly by its people. He refused every gift of money or goods sent to him. Xianzu heard of this and praised him. He was again made Palace Attendant and high minister of the central capital, and received a thousand bolts of silk and a thousand sheep. He was sent out as inspector of Ji Province, retaining his former general's rank. Yun governed attentively and understood those under him so well that the whole province asked to give five chi of silk and five sheng of grain per household in gratitude for his kindness. Gaozu praised him and transferred him to serve as Bearer of the Staff, commander of military affairs in Shaanxi, Grand General Who Conquers the South, commander of Chang'an Garrison, and inspector of Yong Province. Yun was upright and careful, gave close attention to common lawsuits, checked the powerful, and brought banditry to an end; more than a thousand people in the province praised him in verse. Empress Dowager Wenming praised him and gave him a thousand bolts of silk. In Taihe year 5 he died in office in the province. In his last instructions he ordered a simple burial and forbade the acceptance of funerary gifts. His sons carried out his wishes. When his coffin reached the capital, the emperor came in person and wept bitterly over him; Yun was posthumously restored to his offices and titled Kang. He was buried alongside the Jinling mausoleum at Yunzhong. Yun's eldest son Cheng, styled Daozhen, loved learning from an early age. After Prince Kang died, Cheng became known for filial devotion in mourning. He inherited the fief and was given the added rank Grand General Who Conquers the North. Under Gaozu, when the Rouran raided the frontier, Cheng was made Bearer of the Staff and commander of the northern expedition against them. The Rouran fled. Later, when the Di and Qiang rebelled, he was appointed commander of military affairs in Liang, Yi, and Jing provinces, Grand General Who Conquers the South, and inspector of Liang Province. Empress Dowager Wenming received Cheng, admonished him, then turned to Secretariat Director Li Chong. "This young man's bearing is splendid and his speech is gentle; he will become a leader of the imperial clan. On this mission he will surely satisfy me. Remember this: I do not misjudge men." The Di leaders in Liang Province, including Yang Zhongxian, the brothers Poluo and Yang Bu, and Fu Chipan, trusted in the rugged frontier and had long lived as mountain raiders. When Cheng arrived, he studied their customs and coaxed them into allegiance. He sent Poluo to court, made Zhongxian deputy commander at Xuncheng, Yang Bu governor of Guangye, and Chipan deputy commander at Gudao, and used the other chiefs according to their abilities. Those who submitted were rewarded, those who resisted were punished; Qiuchi was pacified and the southwest came over. He was additionally made Palace Attendant and given a set of robes and a riding horse in recognition of his skill. Later he became Grand General Who Conquers the East, opened his office, and served as inspector of Xu Province, earning a strong record of achievement. He came to the capital for court audience and was received in the Hall of Imperial Trust. Gaozu asked Cheng, "When Zheng Zichan cast the penal code, Shu Xiang of Jin criticized him. Both were worthy men; in the end, who was right?" Cheng replied, "Zheng was weak and hemmed in by powerful neighbors. The people could not be controlled without punishments, so Zichan cast the laws to show authority. Though it violated ancient form, it fit the needs of the moment. Zichan adapted to his age and helped the world, so he was right. Shu Xiang's criticism showed that he had not forgotten antiquity; one could discuss principle with him, but not expedience." Gaozu said, "Rencheng must wish to be Wei's Zichan." Cheng replied, "Zichan's way suited his time, and his name passed into the histories. I am mediocre and shallow. How could I dare compare myself to him? Your Majesty now makes the four seas your household and uses civil virtue to embrace the realm, but beyond the river resistance remains, and script and carriage tracks are not yet one. People in a late age are easy to subdue by force and hard to govern by ritual. In my foolish view, Zichan's methods should still be used for a time; once unity is complete, then the Way can transform them." Gaozu was then intent on reform, and he deeply approved Cheng's answer. Smiling, he said, "Without Rencheng, no one would understand the essence of transformation. I am just beginning to remake the court's institutions; Rencheng and I shall share in a work for ten thousand generations." Later Cheng was summoned as Director of the Secretariat and then made Director of the Masters of Writing. When Xiao Ze sent Yu Bi to court, Bi found Cheng's speech forceful and elegant and his bearing refined. He told Reception Gentleman Zhang Yi, "The former Rencheng of Wei was known for arms; this Rencheng of Wei is admired for culture." At that time the court invited the imperial kin, from sons of the four temples down to great-great-grandsons, to a clan banquet in the Hall of Imperial Trust. They were seated not by rank but by ancestral order, using the rites of one family. Gaozu said, "The rites are finished. I want each kinsman to state his aspirations; let each compose a poem." He specially ordered Cheng to compose linked seven-character rhymes. Cheng and Gaozu traded verses in playful contest until they were thoroughly delighted, stopping only late at night. Later Gaozu publicly presented plans for a southern campaign, while actually planning the capital move. Fasting in the left chamber of the Mingtang, he had Grand Director of Ceremonies Wang Chen personally divine by turtle and milfoil about the campaign; the omen was Revolution. Gaozu said, "This is the hexagram by which Tang and Wu changed the mandate, obeying Heaven and answering the people." None of the ministers dared speak. Cheng stepped forward. "In the Changes, Revolution means change. When Tang and Wu obeyed Heaven, answered the people, and changed the mandate between ruler and minister, this hexagram was auspicious. Your Majesty already possesses the realm, with shining succession through many generations. Today the divination is for a campaign; it may mean attacking rebels, but it cannot mean changing the mandate. This is not the hexagram for a reigning lord, and it cannot be taken as wholly auspicious." Gaozu said sternly, "The Image says, 'The great man changes like a tiger.' How can you say it is not auspicious?" Cheng replied, "Your Majesty's dragon rise has long been established; how can it be compared to a tiger's change?" Gaozu's face darkened. "The state is my state. Does Rencheng mean to obstruct everyone?" Cheng said, "I know well that the state is Your Majesty's, but I am its servant and son. Since I have been admitted to counsel, I dare give all my foolish sincerity." Gaozu was determined to proceed and disliked Cheng's answer, but after a long while he relented. "Each has stated his mind; what harm is there?" After returning to the palace, Gaozu immediately summoned Cheng. Before Cheng had mounted the steps, Gaozu called to him from afar, "About that Revolution hexagram: I want to discuss it further. In the Mingtang, I was angry because I feared everyone would start speaking at once and block my great plan, so I put on a stern face to frighten the civil and military officials. I trust you understood my intent." Then he said to Cheng privately, "I know very well that today's undertaking is not easy. Our state rose in the north and later settled at Pingcheng. Though we possess the empire, its script and roads are not yet unified; this is a place for military power, not civil administration. Changing customs and habits here is truly difficult. The Xiao and Han passes are an imperial seat, and the He and Luo region is a royal home. If we use this great move to establish ourselves splendidly in the Central Plain, what does Rencheng think?" Cheng replied, "The Yi and Luo region lies at the center, the seat shared by all under Heaven. If Your Majesty governs China from there and brings peace to the nine regions, the people will surely rejoice when they hear it." Gaozu said, "The northerners cling to their homeland. If they suddenly hear that the capital is to be moved, they are bound to be alarmed and unsettled." Cheng replied, "This is an extraordinary matter, beyond the understanding of ordinary men. It only needs Your Majesty's decision; what can this crowd do about it?" Gaozu said, "Rencheng is truly my Zifang." He was promoted to Grand General Who Pacifies the Army and Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, while concurrently serving as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs. When the emperor went to Luoyang and settled on moving the capital, Gaozu issued an edict: "The decision to relocate must be discussed with the officials. Rencheng should be sent by courier to Dai to ask the officials there and discuss whether the move is acceptable. Recently we discussed transformation; now this is transformation in the true sense. Let the prince exert himself." When he arrived at the old capital of Dai, all who heard the relocation edict were shocked and alarmed. Cheng cited examples from antiquity and recent times, explaining the matter patiently, and only then did everyone understand and accept it. Cheng then hurried south to report back, meeting the emperor at Huatai. Gaozu was delighted. "Without Rencheng, my undertaking could not have succeeded." He accompanied the emperor to Ye Palace and was appointed Minister of Personnel. When the emperor went to Dai and toured the north, Cheng was left to review and rank the old officials. At that time in Wei, from dukes and marquises down to appointed officials, there were often tens of thousands of supernumerary men, idle and without duties. Cheng classified them into three grades, weighed their strengths and weaknesses, and used each according to his ability; no one complained. When the emperor returned to Luoyang, Cheng again served concurrently as Right Vice Director. When Gaozu reached Beimang, he went on to Hongchi, ordered Cheng to attend him aboard the imperial boat, and composed poems there to express his thoughts. Gaozu said, "Last night I dreamed of an old man with white hair and temples. His cap and robes were properly arranged, and he bowed as he stood on the left side of the road. I was surprised and asked who he was. He said he was Xi Shao, Palace Attendant of Jin, and had come to welcome me. His spirit seemed humble and apprehensive, as though he had something to ask." Cheng replied, "During the disorders of Jin, Xi Shao shielded his lord with his own body and died at the emperor's side; he was a loyal minister of Jin. Bigan suffered King Zhou's cruelty and had his heart cut out for his loyal remonstrance; he may be called a worthy man of Yin. Both men died in service to their rulers, and both of their tombs lie beside the road. Yet as Your Majesty traveled, you passed the ruins of Yin and mourned Bigan, but when you reached Luoyang you passed over Xi Shao. He must have sought your favor and moved you through a dream." Gaozu said, "What virtue do I possess, that I could move a worthy man in the unseen world? Still, I have truly wished to honor former worthies and make loyalty and righteousness shine. Bigan and Xi Shao were both faithful heroes of antiquity, but I gave Bigan rich attention and Xi Shao only slight rites. I am ashamed of this. Since this dream has occurred, perhaps it is just as Rencheng says." He then searched for the site of Xi Shao's tomb and sent envoys to mourn and sacrifice there. After Xiao Luan killed Xiao Zhaoye and took power, Cao Hu, Zhaoye's Inspector of Yongzhou, asked to surrender Xiangyang. Gaozu sent out several generals and was preparing to go there in person. Yuzhou then reported that no further envoy had come from Hu to confirm his sincerity. Gaozu summoned Cheng, Yuan Xi the Prince of Xianyang, Yuan Xie the Prince of Pengcheng, Situ Feng Dan, Sikong Mu Liang, General Who Guards the South Li Chong, and others to discuss the matter. Gaozu said, "Recently I received a report from the border province saying that Xiangyang longed for our transforming rule, and I was about to take the imperial carriage to the Jiang and Mian to support them. Now another report says there has been no later message. So, on the question of going or staying, what do you finally advise?" Xi and the others were divided, some saying they should go and others saying they should stop. Gaozu said, "Everyone is arguing at once and their opinions differ; I do not know whose advice to follow. If we are to examine fully the case for going and the case for staying, so that both argument and principle are clear, we should set up opposing sides to draw each other out. Rencheng and the General Who Guards the South may argue for staying, and I will argue for going. Let the lords sit and hear the merits of each side, and then follow the better case." Gaozu then said, "Let the two worthies state the plan for staying." Li Chong replied, "We only think that the retinue has just been organized, the people are content with peace, and the supposed supporters inside have not been confirmed. We should not set out lightly." Gaozu said, "Xiangyang's offer of submission may well be false. I also know that the people newly moved to the capital should not be burdened with service. But if their surrender is genuine, we should take advantage of their willingness to attach themselves to us. At best, we might hold an assembly at Kuaiji; at least, we could bring the land north of the Yangzi roughly under control. If the offer is false, we can still tour Huai and Chu, inquire into the people's hardships, and let the people there see where the ruler's virtue lies. What harm would that do, that we should shrink from this single move? If the surrender is real and we halt without receiving and reassuring them, would that not block their sincere submission and ruin my larger plan?" Cheng said, "If the surrender report were reliable, there should be a formal memorial and pledge. But since the envoy returned, there has been only silence and no further message. Its falseness is obvious. The people moved from Dai still long for their old home. They have only just reached Luoyang with their families and dependents; they have not even a single-raftered house to live in, and their households lack a bare measure of grain. If we drive them bitterly to war, weeping before drawn blades, this will hardly be an army marching in joy. This region is only newly founded, and the spring labors are just beginning. It is the time for the people to build the city walls and for farmers to spend their strength in the fields. We should defer punishment over there and show kindness to the common people here. Besides, the armies have already been sent in support; there is no need to rush in person to receive an unverified surrender. If the offer is genuine, our forces are sufficient to receive and pacify them. Once Xiangyang and the Mian region have been secured, the emperor can move then. To make this hard journey without cause, only to go and return in vain, would damage imperial majesty and embolden the rebels. I ask Your Majesty to remember the hardships Pan Geng faced when he first moved the capital, and to heed the poet's deepest praise in "You Geng": settle the new city and bring comfort to the people." But Sikong Mu Liang thought they should go, and the high ministers all agreed with him. Cheng said to Liang, "Outside, when you saw the banners and axes already set out, you looked worried; whenever you discussed it, you did not want this expedition. How can you now say such things before His Majesty? To say one thing to a man's face and another behind his back borders on deceitful flattery. That is not the virtue of one who debates principle, and it falls short of the bearing of a statesman. If the state is thrown off balance, it will be because of flatterers like you." Li Chong said, "The Prince of Rencheng can truly be called loyal to the state. I hope Your Majesty will weigh his words carefully. Outside court, all of us fear the campaign. High and low have not conferred, yet we say the same thing. I beg Your Majesty to decide what is right." Gaozu said, "Rencheng made that argument just because you gentlemen sided with me. Are all who disagree with me necessarily loyal men with a penetrating grasp of danger and security? Small loyalty is the enemy of great loyalty. Is this not something like that?" Cheng said, "I am foolish and dim and do not understand great principles. What I say may be only small loyalty, but it is the full measure of my poor sincerity. I do not know: what, in the end, is great loyalty based on?" Gaozu said, "If Rencheng held the office of an Excellency, he would want great loyalty to belong to himself." Cheng replied, "My talent is not fit to support the highest offices, and my wisdom is not enough to season the cauldron of state. But if I undeservedly held an Excellency's place, I hope I would act according to the office and not betray my poor intentions." Gaozu burst out laughing. Cheng then said to Liang, "Long ago, in front of Emperor Wu of Han, Ji An accused Gongsun Hong to his face of eating coarse grain and sleeping under a plain cloth quilt as a fraud. At the time, Gongsun humbly yielded and put himself below him. Emperor Wu admired Ji An for utmost loyalty and Gongsun for elder virtue, and both men were praised as worthy. Since your conduct can equal that of men of old, I hope you will remember the elder's example." Gaozu laughed. "Rencheng wants to compare himself to Ji An. Besides, your words concerned the Duke, and we do not yet know who is right or wrong. Why rush to apologize to the Minister of Works?" The emperor then went south on campaign. When the five ranks of nobility were instituted, his fief was set at one thousand households. Later he accompanied the campaign to Xuanhu, but returned to the capital because of serious illness. The emperor saw him off on the bank of the Ru River, composing poems as they parted. When the emperor returned to Luoyang, he received the princes, dukes, and attendant ministers in Qinghui Hall. Gaozu said, "Since this hall was completed, I have not yet held a proper feast here with the princes and dukes. Now that the eastern pavilion and side halls have roughly been completed, I want to go through them today with you worthies, ascending every height and entering every small place." They then went to the Liuhua Canal. Gaozu said, "This winding water has meaning too. It draws on the Way of Qian, which completes things by bending and leaves all things unobstructed." Next they went to the Xifan Pond. Gaozu said, "There are fine fish in this pond as well." Cheng said, "This is what the poem means: "The fish are there among the weeds; large are their heads."" Gaozu said, "Let us instead take the line, "The king is at the Spirit Pond; it is full, and the fish leap."" Next they went to the Hall for Observing Virtue. Gaozu said, "Archery is used to observe virtue, so I gave it this name." Next they went to the Ningxian Hall. Gaozu said, "A name must have meaning. This one draws on the idea of the Master at leisure. One must not indulge in luxury and forget thrift, or rest in safety and forget danger. That is why I built the Thatched Hall behind it." He said to Li Chong, "The eastern gallery is called Buyuan, and the western one Youkai. Although this hall has no ruler equal to Tang Yao, you gentlemen should not be ashamed before Yuan and Kai." Chong replied, "Since I have encountered a ruler like Tang Yao, I dare not refuse the praise of being Yuan or Kai." Gaozu said, "The daylight is fading. For my clansmen there is the duty of continuing the feast into the night, and you gentlemen are about to withdraw though the hour is not far advanced. How can you stay silent and not give us worthy words?" He then ordered Cui Guang and Guo Zuo, Palace Attendants of the Yellow Gates, and Xing Luan, Cui Xiu, and others, Gentlemen for Unrestricted Attendance, to compose poems expressing their thoughts. When the candles were brought in, the dukes and ministers took their leave. Li Chong bowed twice and offered a long-life toast of countless years. Gaozu said, "You used the arrival of the candles as a reason to withdraw, and then offered a toast of countless years. I will answer you with the poem of the Southern Mountain." Gaozu said, "Taking leave when the candles arrive is the rite for those of other surnames; continuing the gathering into the night is the duty of the imperial clan. You gentlemen may go home for now. I and the princes of the imperial clan wish to finish tonight's drinking." He again accompanied the emperor to Ye. After returning to Luoyang, his fief was increased by five hundred households for his work handling communications and affairs. He was dismissed from office over an official matter. Soon he was made acting Minister of Personnel. Mu Tai, Inspector of Hengzhou, plotted rebellion in his province and proposed Yuan Yi, Prince of Yangping and Inspector of Shuozhou, as their leader. Yi reported the situation in a memorial. Gaozu summoned Cheng to Ningxian Hall and said, "I have just received Yangping's memorial. It says that Mu Tai is plotting rebellion and trying to draw in members of the imperial clan. If this is true, the capital has only just been moved, the northerners still cling to the old places, north and south will fall into turmoil, and my Luoyang will not stand. No one but Rencheng can handle this. For my sake, struggle through your illness and go north. If he is weak, go directly and capture or destroy him; if his forces are strong, you may act under imperial authority and mobilize the troops of Bing and Si to wipe him out. I know you are ill, but this is a great matter of state and cannot be declined." Cheng said, "Mu Tai and the others are foolish and confused. They do this only from attachment to their old home; they have no long-term plan. I am timid and weak, but I do not fear men like these. Though I am ill and worn down, how could I dare refuse? I will devote all my heart and strength, even unto death. I ask Your Majesty not to worry." Gaozu laughed. "With Rencheng making this trip, what do I have left to worry about?" He then granted Cheng the staff, bronze tiger tally and bamboo envoy tally, imperial weapons and attendants, and had him administer Hengzhou affairs. When Cheng reached Yanmen, the governor reported by night that Mu Tai had gathered his followers and gone west to join Yangping. Men were assembling below the city, and bows and weapons were everywhere. On hearing this, Cheng advanced at once. Right Aide Meng Bin said, "The situation is uncertain. We should obey the edict, summon the troops of Bing and Si, and only then proceed carefully." Cheng said, "If Tai has truly mounted a rebellion, he should be holding a strong city; instead he has gone to meet Yangping. From his conduct, his position seems weak. Since Tai is not opposing us directly, it would be wrong to call up troops without cause. If we simply get there quickly and hold things down, the people will settle by themselves." He then doubled his stages, pressed forward, and caught them by surprise. He also sent Li Huan, Investigating Censor for the Bureau of Evaluation, ahead. When Li Huan arrived he immediately captured Tai, and the people were reassured. They tracked down his associates and captured all the offenders. Lu Rui, Duke of Julu, Yuan Long, Marquis of Anle, and more than a hundred others were imprisoned. Cheng reported the full case in a memorial. Gaozu read it with great delight, summoned the high ministers and officials, showed them the memorial, and said, "My Rencheng may truly be called a minister of state. In investigating this case, even Gaoyao himself could not have surpassed him." He turned to the Prince of Xianyang and the others. "Had you been in his place, you could not have managed this." Soon afterward the emperor went to Pingcheng and commended Cheng: "Rencheng's mission has fully answered the trust placed in him from afar." Cheng replied, "Your Majesty's awe reaches far; the guilty had nowhere to escape punishment. What effort of mine was there?" When the rebels were presented, not one claimed to have been wronged, and everyone at the time marveled. Gaozu turned to his attendants and said, "Long ago Confucius said, "In hearing lawsuits I am no different from others; what matters is making it so there are no lawsuits. But a sage's handling of cases is hardly something ordinary men can match. Today I have seen what it means to leave no one with a grievance." He made Cheng a full Minister of State Affairs. When the emperor campaigned south, Cheng was left in charge of the capital and again concurrently served as Right Vice Director. Cheng memorialized asking to contribute one year of his fief income in cloth and silk to military supplies; by edict the court accepted half. When Gaozu went to Ye, the Shuzhe branch of the Gaoche rebelled, and the emperor was about to campaign against them personally. Cheng sent a memorial remonstrating that the emperor should not go in person. Then Yuan Ji, Prince of Jiangyang, pacified them, and the expedition was called off. When Gaozu returned to Luoyang, he received the high ministers. Gaozu said, "Ritual instruction comes first in ordering the state. Since I left the capital, has ritual instruction been renewed day by day, or not?" Cheng replied, "I believe it has been renewed day by day." Gaozu said, "Yesterday as I entered the city, I saw women on carts wearing caps and little short jackets. If this is going on, why has the Ministry failed to investigate?" Cheng said, "Those wearing them are still fewer than those who are not." Gaozu said, "That is astonishing! Does Rencheng mean he wants all of them to wear such things? Is this what is meant by a single word being able to ruin a state? Have the historian record it." He also said, "Rulers do not receive assistants dropped down from Heaven; they select talented men and employ them. I made a mistake in appointing men, allowing this strange business with a group of women. The officials must be reviewed and selected again. Is Rencheng in the department to uphold the governing order of the realm, or merely to sign papers?" Cheng said, "In truth, I am only signing papers." Gaozu said, "If that is so, one clerk would be enough. Why would we need Rencheng?" He also said, "I sent a palace attendant to proclaim the edict. Why did you let petty men hear it?" Cheng said, "At the time there were capable officials, but they too were far from the posted proclamation." Gaozu said, "If they were far away, they could not have heard it; if they heard it, they were not far away. Since they heard the edict, they should have understood the principle." The ministers left in charge of the capital then removed their caps and apologized for their fault. Soon he was appointed Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs. Xiao Baojuan sent his Grand Commandant Chen Xianda to invade Hanyang. At the time Gaozu was ill, and he summoned Cheng to Qinghui Hall. The edict said, "Xianda has invaded and thrown Mianyang into disorder. Unless I go in person, no one will repel this rebel. My illness has dragged on for years, and my strength is spent. If anything unexpected happens, I entrust the great affairs to Rencheng. For this campaign, Rencheng must accompany me." Cheng replied through tears, "I will devote all the strength of my limbs and repay Your Majesty with my life." He then accompanied the emperor on the southern campaign. When Gaozu died, Cheng received his final charge. At the start of Shizong's reign, a defector named Yan Shumao accused Wang Su, Director of the Department of State Affairs, of sending Kong Sida to communicate secretly with Baojuan and plot rebellion. Baojuan, he said, had sent Yu Gongxi with an edict for Su; after Gongxi returned south, Su and Pei Shuye exchanged horses as tokens. Cheng believed the accusation, memorialized that Su was about to rebel, and immediately detained him. The princes of Xianyang and Beihai memorialized that Cheng had detained a chief minister on his own authority, and Cheng was dismissed and sent home. Soon he was sent out as General Who Pacifies the West and Inspector of Liangzhou. He declined because his mother was elderly. He was appointed General Who Pacifies the East and Inspector of Xiangzhou, but again firmly refused. His appointment was changed to General Who Pacifies the West and Inspector of Yongzhou. Soon he was summoned to attend the late-autumn martial review. He was appointed Commander of all military affairs in Huainan, Grand General Who Guards the South with an open office, and Inspector of Yangzhou. On taking office, he marked and protected Sunshu Ao's tomb and destroyed the temple of Jiang Ziwen. He repeatedly memorialized urging a southern campaign, but Shizong would not allow it. Again citing his mother's age, he asked to be relieved of the province, but the request was shelved without response. He was additionally made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary. Cheng memorialized, "I took part in the instruction of the former court and have long lived under its rules; I have heard something of its words and precedents. In earlier days at Heng and Dai, I was personally familiar with the imperial clan, and there was no lack of instruction, inquiry, and court discussion. Whenever I sat in attendance, the former emperor always kept the texts and classics in mind and made the ritual classics his concern; the rules of conduct were never neglected. After the move to the central capital, ritual instruction flourished. Matters concerning the imperial clan's standards were often entrusted to me, and I bore responsibility for evaluating candidates for the Four Gates school. Since the former emperor passed away, there has been no time to restore these institutions. The school palace bears the Four Gates name in vain, the clansmen lack their seasonal studies, and the line of students is on the verge of disappearing. Whenever I think of this, I am privately grieved. I humbly think that Your Majesty's strategy is broad and far-reaching, and with few urgent affairs on the frontiers, this is the moment for secure repose. Why, in an age of great peace, should the lament for neglected students arise? Why, in days of sage enlightenment, should the instruction of the imperial clan be lacking? In my foolish view, the offices should be ordered to restore the imperial clan school and reopen the Four Gates instruction, so that a clan now close to decline may improve day by day and month by month." The edict said, "The education of noble sons has been a great institution since antiquity, and instruction in the state schools should not long be abandoned. The Department may consider what is suitable and restore it." Cheng again memorialized that his mother was ill and asked to be relieved of his province, but this was not allowed. When Xiao Yan's general Zhang Xiaozhi captured the Yiling Garrison, Cheng sent Cheng Xing, General Who Assists the State, with infantry and cavalry to attack. Cheng Xing defeated him badly, recovered Yiling, and Xiaozhi fled. He also sent Qi Daoxian, commander of Changfeng Garrison, to attack Xiao Yan's Yinshan Garrison. Qi defeated it and beheaded its commander Mei Xingzu, General Who Rouses Dragons and Marquis of Duting. He then pressed on to attack Baigao Garrison, defeated it as well, and beheaded Wu Daoshuang, General Who Pacifies the North and Marquis within the Passes. Cheng memorialized, "Xiao Yan has repeatedly breached Dongguan, intending to make Chaohu overflow. The lake is over four hundred li in circuit, and where Dongguan meets the river it is only a few dozen paces wide. If the rebels succeed and the great lake pours out, all our Huainan garrisons will suffer the fate of Jinyang. Moreover, Wu and Chu are skilled in water warfare. If they flood while raiding, Huainan will no longer be ours. Shouyang lies more than five hundred li from the river, and the people are terrified, all fearing flood damage. If we use the people's wishes, strike the enemy's weak point, prearrange the provinces, gather troops and horses, and assemble them in early autumn, then the southern channel can become a ford for watering our horses, and Huo Ridge a height from which we look out at ease. Opportunity must be answered, and planning must begin early. Even if complete unification cannot be guaranteed, the lands west of the Yangzi will at least be secure. If we hesitate and delay instead of eliminating the threat, then once the barriers are finished and the waters rise to the hills, the people and garrisons of the plains will become fish." An edict mobilized twenty thousand men and fifteen hundred horses from Ji, Ding, Ying, Xiang, Bing, and Ji provinces, ordering them to assemble in Huainan by mid-autumn. Together with Shouyang's existing thirty thousand troops, they were placed under Cheng's command. Earlier, the court had planned a southern campaign, placing Xiao Baoyin at Dongcheng as Inspector of Eastern Yangzhou and Chen Bozhi at Yangshi as Inspector of Jiangzhou. Cheng was put in overall command of the two positions. At this point he ordered the troops forward. Dongguan controlled the water flow, and Daxian was a crucial pass. If Dongguan released the water, Yangshi and Hefei would be in immediate danger; if Daxian was ignored, Liyang could use the pass as support. The Huailing land route and the Jiushan water route both had to be included in the plan. He therefore sent Fu Shuyan, Wang Shennian, and other commanders to advance to Daxian, Dongguan, Jiushan, and Huailing. The generals divided the sectors, hurried to occupy them, and linked the main forces in a continuous line. Wang Shennian captured Guanyao and Yingchuan and beheaded Fei Ni, one of Xiao Yan's commanders. Ning Shuo General Wei Hui and Longxiang General Li Boyou were still holding Daxian. Cheng sent Dang Fazong, Fu Shuyan, and other commanders forward to take it. They then besieged Baita and Qiancheng, which fled and collapsed within a few days. Xiao Yan's Qingxi Garrison scattered at the news. Sima Mingsu, Xiao Yan's Inspector of Xuzhou, led three thousand men to reinforce Jiushan; Pan Bolin, Chief Clerk of Xuzhou, planned to hold Huailing; and Ning Shuo General Wang Xie relied on the strong position at Jiaocheng. Dang Fazong advanced, captured Jiaocheng, broke Huailing, captured Mingsu, and beheaded Bolin. Wang Houqiang, their Governor of Jiyin, and Pei Sui, Governor of Lujiang, also fled. The edict to Cheng said, "General, your civil virtue shines within and your military achievements resound abroad. You have displayed a grand strategy and are about to sweep away Jiang and Wu. As soon as the long banners were unfurled, the rebels lost heart; as the elite troops began to advance, Dongguan was rolled up like a mat. I expect the rivers and lakes to be pacified very soon. The heads and captives you sent have all been reported." Earlier, after Cheng had marched out, Xiao Yan's general Jiang Qingzhen attacked and occupied the outer wall of Shouchun, but Xiao Baoyin, Prince of Qi, attacked and drove him away. Chief Clerk Wei Zuan was dismissed for this, while Cheng was not held responsible because he was away. Cheng then attacked Zhongli. Another edict said, "If Zhongli runs out of food, it can surely be taken before the third month; but if matters reach the fourth month, the Huai will rise and boats will pass freely. Weigh this carefully. The earlier victory was truly due to your planning, General, and that merit stands secure. If high water makes the objective difficult, you may choose a safer plan. Do not be blinded by advantage, fail to achieve the goal, and leave regret for later." Xiao Yan's generals Zhang Huishao, Yin Xian, Zhao Jingyue, Zhang Jingren, and others led five thousand men escorting grain to Zhongli. Cheng sent Wang Zu, Liu Sizu, and other commanders to intercept Huishao and his men, defeating them badly. They captured Huishao, Yin Xian, Jingren, Shi Wenyuan, their Colonel of Garrison Cavalry, and twenty-seven officers of army commander rank or higher. Soon afterward rain came, the Huai rose sharply, and Cheng withdrew to Shouchun. The retreat became disordered, and he lost more than four thousand men. He repeatedly memorialized asking to be relieved of his province, but Shizong refused. The officials memorialized that the returning army had lost its route; Cheng was stripped of his open office and demoted three ranks. At the time Xiao Yan sent a letter requesting an exchange for Zhang Huishao. Cheng memorialized that the request should not be allowed, and the edict referred it to the Eight Seats for conference. Jia, Prince of Guangyang and Director of the Department of State Affairs, and others memorialized that Zhang Huishao should be returned, and the edict allowed it. Later, as expected, he raided the border again. Cheng was transferred to Grand General Who Guards the North and Inspector of Dingzhou. The people had long suffered from arbitrary levies, which previous governors and administrators had failed to abolish. Cheng reduced many of them, and the people rejoiced and relied on him. He also clarified rules for promotion, demotion, reward, and punishment; memorialized to reduce public parkland and give it to poor households without livelihoods; and banned the production of cloth and silk unfit for clothing. When his mother, Grand Consort Meng, died, he wasted away in mourning, and his contemporaries praised him for it. After the mourning period ended, he was appointed Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent. At that time Gao Zhao controlled the court and was suspicious of worthy imperial relatives. Cheng was slandered and isolated by Gao Zhao and constantly feared for his life, so he drank heavily all day to appear ruined and useless. His strange, excessive behavior was taken at the time for madness. When Shizong died at night, events were sudden and confused. Gao Zhao held troops outside, Suzong was still a child, and both court and countryside were uneasy. Cheng had been kept at a distance and excluded from confidential affairs, but the court's hopes rested on him. Yu Zhong, Commander of the Guards, Cui Guang, Palace Attendant, and others memorialized that Cheng be made Director of the Department of State Affairs, and everyone gladly accepted this. He was also made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand General of Agile Cavalry; soon he was promoted to Minister of Works with the added title Palace Attendant, and shortly afterward was ordered to concurrently direct the Department of State Affairs. Earlier, at the end of the Zhengshi era, an edict raised all offices by one grade, but the officials implementing it misunderstood the intent, so inspectors, governors, and magistrates were excluded. Cheng memorialized, "I humbly think that when imperial favor rose like gathering clouds and reached the hundred offices, officials inside and outside the court looked toward renewed honor and rejoiced together. Yet the promotion did not reach governors and magistrates, and for ten years grievances and appeals have continued without end. Feng Hui came in from Zhenyuan General and Anzhou to serve as Chief Clerk to the Grand Commandant, while Yuan Kuang came in from Zhenglu General and Hengzhou to serve as Chamberlain for the Imperial Clan. Both appointments occurred before the earlier edict. These cases fully show the principle by which they should receive the benefit. Moreover, provincial assistants, private retainers who had ceased service, subordinate officers, and commandery deputies all received the court's favor and shared in the honor at the time. But assistants come forward through their chiefs. For the chiefs to receive nothing while their subordinates alone benefit abandons the root and rewards the branch; in my foolish view this is not just. I therefore ask that inspectors, governors, and magistrates be treated according to the precedents of Feng Hui and Yuan Kuang and included within the general scope, above fulfilling the original edict's words about the hundred offices, and below satisfying the hearts of the people who have appealed." The edict said, "From now on, internal and external matters already handled under the former reign may not be reported again." Cheng memorialized, "I have heard that Yao hung up the remonstrance drum and Shun set up the criticism post, both to widen their hearing and sight among even the humblest people and let the ruler's fourfold hearing reach all under Heaven. Taizu founded the dynasty and his transforming rule spread far. Sage rulers have succeeded one another, down to the ninth emperor today. Their radiance has shone one after another; whether in decline or flourishing, the principle is the same. Granting and withholding follow the times, and the Way has no fixed form. They thirsted for reflection on their faults and valued speech at a thousand pieces of gold; thus ours was called a court without taboos, surpassing the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors. Gaozu inherited the throne while young, and Empress Wenming assisted the government. They changed offices and laws, yet did not violate classical norms. When the Compassionate Sage held court, her maternal example covered the realm. She issued merciful orders and attended to stalled cases, so the deeply wronged looked up to sun and moon even from the Nine Springs, and the slightly aggrieved hoped for a slant of light beneath the overturned basin. Now to block such cases as belonging to the former reign and limit them by one rule may be meant as obedience, but it truly violates the people's deepest hopes. As a matter of humble receptiveness, it also departs from the old institutions. I have examined those who carry grievances and seek justice; some cases have lasted through several reigns. A difference of a hair's breadth should be corrected quickly; if an error becomes a thousand li, even a four-horse team cannot catch it. Thus ritual can be reduced or augmented, affairs can be approved or rejected, fathers have sons who argue with them, and rulers have ministers who remonstrate. If zithers and lutes are out of tune, they should be adjusted. Thus, in the argument over blocking rivers, a small opening lets them flow; and as for speech in the village schools, blocking it ruins the state. How much more when people are presenting grievances: how can they be suppressed merely because they concern a former reign? Those wronged under the former reign were not wronged deliberately by the throne. Sometimes officials were moved by favoritism or hatred, sometimes clerks were corrupt and biased, and empty paperwork produced legal judgments that misled the court. Such obstructed grievances are all the more pitiful. If there is risk of excess, I would rather err on the side of irregular openness. I beg that the present order be withdrawn and that we return to the previous edict." The edict said, "I have reviewed the memorial and deeply understand your wish to assist the throne. The Three Sovereigns followed different paths and the Five Ages different customs; why must the institutions of one period all be revised? If one says that formal texts merely express an intention and that the principle may be extended, then how could similar cases not all come forward to be taken up? Let the former system be followed." Cheng submitted one fascicle each of Imperial Admonitions, Clan Regulations, and Explanatory Glosses, hoping the Empress Dowager would read them and consider their value for admonition. He also submitted ten recommendations for measures that should be revived to benefit the state and aid the people. First: statutes, measures, weights, and balances differ between public and private use and should be unified. Second: schools should be promoted to clarify the rules for demotion and promotion. Third: fallen lines should be revived and extinct lines continued, with each official recommending those he knows. Fourth: beyond the five regular levies, the people should not be burdened, and labor service should not exceed three days. Fifth: officials who govern the people must be subject to promotion and demotion, so that reward and punishment are clear. Sixth: fugitives whose obligations are being paid by substitutes, and whose absence or return has lasted for years, should be allowed to settle where they are, unless they are registered artisans. Seventh: cases of border soldiers who flee, or who have truly been captured or killed, must be carefully investigated; if the three chiefs or close relatives truly concealed the facts, collect the substitute payments from them; if they did not conceal them, do not prosecute. Eighth: hereditary artisan and merchant households are again being charged rents and levies beyond what they can bear. I request that they be exempted so they can concentrate on their work. Ninth: the three chiefs, in suppressing crime, should not command across boundaries; where there are too few households, they should be merged with nearby units. Tenth: the Yulin and Huben guards may be sent temporarily to fight when there is trouble on the frontier, but regular garrison duty should be assigned to tribal troops in their place. Empress Dowager Ling sent his memorial down for discussion by the officials, who agreed on some points and disagreed on others. At the time the four Central Gentleman-General commands had too few weak troops to protect the capital. Cheng proposed that the Eastern Center be linked with Yingyang Commandery, the Southern Center with Luyang, the Western Center with Hengnong, and the Northern Center with Henei; that qualified close and worthy men of the second and third ranks be chosen to hold them; that nonurgent works be reduced; and that strong troops be assigned. This, he said, would deepen the roots, strengthen the base, strengthen the trunk, and weaken the branches. Empress Dowager Ling initially intended to follow the proposal, but later the discussants disagreed, so it was dropped. Cheng memorialized again, "To secure the root, it must be strengthened; to guard against small dangers, one must prepare in advance. Thus even in civil affairs, military power is not forgotten. How much more now, when the southern Man remain fierce and northern enemies repeatedly combine. Future events are hard to foresee, and the situation resembles past upheavals. If a sudden uprising breaks out and shakes the passes and capital region, how can the weak troops of the four offices defend against it? In peaceful times one may rely on security, but to leave matters this way for long is not good policy. In my foolish view, the Gentleman Generals should command troops while also overseeing civil duties; this is where offices can be reduced while real salaries are preserved. I ask that we return to the earlier plan of increasing troops and strengthening the titles. If the generals' posts are weighty, their sense of obligation will deepen; if army and commandery depend on one another, inner and outer defenses will both be supplied. The court will have no worries on any side, and criminals will lose hope of taking advantage." In the end the proposal was not accepted. He also noted that exiles newly sent to distant garrisons lacked clothing and food and often died, so he memorialized that they and their families be given a year's grain. This was approved. Soon afterward he asked to be relieved because of illness, but this was not allowed. When Xiao Yan dammed the Huai at Fushan to flood Shouchun, Cheng was appointed Bearer of the Staff, Grand General, and Grand Commander of the southern campaign armies, with orders to lead one hundred thousand men out through Peng and Song. Soon the Huai dam collapsed on its own, and the campaign did not proceed. Cheng believed that commanders for the northern frontier garrisons were being chosen too lightly. Fearing that raiders would threaten the border and endanger the imperial tombs, he memorialized asking that garrison commanders be selected more carefully and defenses tightened, but the edict did not accept this. When the raiders entered and reached the old capital, many garrison commanders proved unfit, rebellions broke out in many places, and the imperial tombs were threatened, exactly as Cheng had feared. Cheng memorialized that the capital's offices and temples were still incomplete, but since the armies had only just settled, the people should not be mobilized. He asked instead to use office laborers and the redemption payments for offenses in Sizhou commanderies and counties punishable by ten strokes to one hundred lashes: each bolt of silk would be commuted to two hundred bricks, so construction could proceed gradually. The edict approved this. The Grand Tutor Yuan Yi, Prince of Qinghe, submitted a memorial about the matter, and it was shelved without being carried out. Cheng also memorialized, "I have heard that rewards must follow the Way, to guard against the schemes of corrupt men; punishments must not be indiscriminate, lest good men be driven into distress. Punishment is a matter of setting a model. One should always extend the three pardons, and only when the law is upheld and the request cannot be granted should punishment be used. Thus in cases great and small, one examines the circumstances; even one person crying out in grievance can diminish the kingly Way. The success or failure of punishments is the source of a state's rise or decline. I have heard privately that Yuan Yong, Minister of Sizhou and Prince of Gaoyang, tortured and killed Han Yuanzhao, Gentleman for Court Audience, and Yao Jingxian, former Recorder of the Chancellery. Although this arose from official business, the facts were not fully investigated. Why do I say this? In an age of great peace, even grasses are not wantonly cut; the compassion shown in "Walking among the Reeds" was proven in the flourishing Zhou. If the crimes of Yuanzhao and the others were clear and death sentences certain, they should have been executed in the marketplace and cast out before the crowd; if the suspicions had not been distinguished and the facts had not been fully examined, officials of their rank should not have died under the cudgel, their lives lightly cut off in a way that injured principle and ruined law. In a previous year the province flogged five men to death in the great marketplace, and when the alleged stolen goods were investigated there was not the slightest evidence. Now its cruelty has once again gone this far. Court and countryside are talking, and everyone is shocked. If life and death lie in the hands of subordinates and cruelty is monopolized by ministers, what use remains for the ruler's authority? Since antiquity began, in bright and enlightened ages, I have never heard of such a thing. King Wu said, "I would not trade one man's life for all under Heaven." This was because he valued human life. I request that the case be given to the Chamberlain for Law Enforcement to investigate, verify the alleged robbery, and examine the grounds for the torture-killings, so that right and wrong become clear and the dead may be vindicated." The edict approved this. Cheng acted according to his office and avoided nothing. He also memorialized eight provisions on the system for allotting reclaimed fields. They were orderly and coherent, and greatly suited the needs of the time. Previously, when the various bureaus needed documents and registers from the Department of State Affairs, the records were lent out. At the time, the Office of Public Carriages regarded the handling of grievance cases as important. It memorialized requesting the original case files. Cheng insisted in a memorial that the Department of State Affairs was the root of government and had to be handled with special caution. All memorialized matters were transmitted through the palace galleries precisely because secrecy was urgent and disclosure had to be prevented. How could something the ancient system treated as weighty now be treated lightly, keeping restrictions inside while loosening them outside? The substance of the case should be copied out and given to the Office of Public Carriages.
2
詔從之。
The edict agreed.
3
西域嚈噠、波斯諸國各因公使，並遺澄駿馬一匹。 澄請付太僕，以充國閑。 詔曰：「王廉貞之德，有過楚相，可敕付廐，以成君子大哉之美。」 御史中尉東平王匡奏請取景明元年以來，內外考簿、吏部除書、中兵勳案并諸殿最，欲以案校竊階盜官之人，靈太后許之。 澄表曰：「臣聞三季之弊，由於煩刑； 火德之興，在於三約。 是以老聃云「法令滋彰，盜賊多有」，又曰「其政察察，其民缺缺」，又曰「天網恢恢，疏而不漏」。 是故欲求治本，莫若省事清心。 昔漢文斷獄四百，幾致刑措，省事所致也。 蕭曹為相，載其清靜畫一之歌，清心之本也。 今欲求之於本，宜以省事為先，使在位羣官，纂蕭曹之心，以毗聖化。 如此，則上下相安，遠近相信，百司不怠，事無愆失。 豈宜擾世教以深文，烹小鮮以煩手哉。 臣竊惟景明之初暨永平之末，內外羣官三經考課。 逮延昌之始，方加黜陟。 五品以上，引之朝堂，親決聖目； 六品以下，例由敕判。 自世宗晏駕，大宥三行，所以蕩除故意，與物更始。 革世之事，方相窮覈，以臣愚見，謂為不可。 又尚書職分，樞機出納。 昔魏明帝卒至尚書門，陳矯亢辭，帝慚而返。 夫以萬乘之重，非所宜行，猶屈一言，慚而回駕，羣官百司，而可相亂乎？ 故陳平不知錢穀之數，邴吉不問僵道之死，當時以為達治，歷代用為美談。 但宜各守其職，思不出位，潔己以勵時，靖恭以致節。 又尋御史之體，風聞是司，至於冒勳妄考，皆有處別，若一處有風謠，即應攝其一簿，研檢虛實，若差舛不同，偽情自露，然後繩以典刑，人孰不服。 豈有移一省之案，取天下之簿，尋兩紀之事，窮革世之尤，如此求過，誰堪其罪！ 斯實聖朝所宜重慎也。」 靈太后納之，乃止。 後遷司徒公，侍中、尚書令如故。 澄又表曰：「伏惟世宗宣武皇帝命將授旗，隨陸啟顙，運籌制勝，淮漢自賓。 節用勞心，志清六合，是故纘武修文，仍世彌盛。 陛下當周康靖治之時，豈得晏安於玄默。 然取外之理，要由內強； 圖人之本，先在自備。 蕭衍雖虐使其民，而窺覦不已。 若遇我虛疲，士民淍窘，賊衍年老志張，思播虺毒，此之弗圖，恐受其病。 伏惟陛下妙齡在位，聖德方昇； 皇太后總御天機，乾乾夕惕。 若留意於負荷，忿車書之未一。 進賢拔能，重官人之舉； 標賞忠清，旌養人之器； 修干戈之用，畜熊虎之士； 愛時鄙財，輕寶重穀。 七八年間，陛下聖略方剛，親王德幹壯茂，將相膂力未衰，愚臣猶堪戎伍，荷戈帶甲之眾蓄銳於今，燕弧冀馬之盛充牣在昔； 又賊衍惡積禍盈，勢不能久，子弟闇悖，釁逆已彰，亂亡之兆，灼然可見。 兼弱有徵，天與不遠，大同之機，宜須蓄備。 昔漢帝力疾，討滅英布； 高皇臥病，親除顯達。 夫以萬乘之主，豈忘宴安，實以侵名亂正，計不得已。 今宜慕二帝之遠圖，以肅寧為大任。 然頃年以來，東西難寇，艱虞之興，首尾連接，雖尋得翦除，亦大損財力。 且飢饉之氓，散亡莫保，收入之賦不增，出用之費彌眾，不愛力以悅民，無豐資以待敵，此臣所以夙夜懷憂，悚息不寧者也。 易曰：「何以守位曰仁，何以聚人曰財。」 故曰：財者，非天不生，非地不長，非時不成，非人不聚。 生聚之由，如此其難； 集人守位，若此之重。 興替之道，焉可不慮。 又古者使民，歲不過三日，食壯者之糧，任老者之智。 此雖太平之法，難卒而因； 然妨民害財，不亦宜戒！ 今墉雉素修，廐庫崇列。 雖府寺膠塾，少有未周，大抵省府粗得庇憇理務，諸寺靈塔俱足致虔講道。 唯明堂辟雍，國禮之大。 來冬司徒兵至，請籌量減徹，專力經營，務令早就。 其廣濟數施之財，酬商互市之弊，凡所營造，自非供御切須，戎仗急要，亦宜微減，以務阜積，庶府無橫損，民有全力。 夫食土簋而媯德昭，寢卑室而禹功盛，章臺麗而楚力衰，阿宮壯而秦財竭，存亡之由，灼然可覩。 願思前王一同之功，畜力聚財，以待時會。」 靈太后銳於繕興，在京師則起永寧、太上公等佛寺，功費不少，外州各造五級佛圖，又數為一切齋會，施物動至萬計。 百姓疲於土木之功，金銀之價為之踊上，削奪百官事力，費損庫藏，兼曲賚左右，日有數千。 澄故有此表。 雖卒不從，常優答禮之。 政無大小，皆引參決。 澄亦盡心匡輔，事有不便於民者，必於諫諍，雖不見用，殷勤不已，內外咸敬憚之。 神龜二年薨，年五十三。 賻布一千二百匹、錢六十萬、蠟四百斤，給東園溫明祕器、朝服一具、衣一襲； 大鴻臚監護喪事，詔百僚會喪； 贈假黃鉞、使持節、都督中外諸軍事、太傅，領太尉公； 加以殊禮，備九錫，依晉大司馬、齊王攸故事； 諡曰文宣王。 澄之葬也，凶飾甚盛。 靈太后親送郊外，停輿悲哭，哀動左右。 百官會赴千餘人，莫不歔欷。 當時以為哀榮之極。
The Hephthalites, Persia, and other countries of the Western Regions each sent Cheng a fine horse through official envoys. Cheng asked that the horses be given to the Grand Coachman and added to the state stables. The edict said, "The Prince's incorrupt virtue surpasses that of the minister of Chu. Let the horses be sent to the stables, completing the great beauty of a gentleman." Kuang, Prince of Dongping and Censor-in-Chief, requested the evaluation registers from inside and outside the court since Jingming year 1, the Ministry of Personnel appointment documents, Central Army merit files, and all best-and-worst assessments, intending to use them to investigate those who had stolen ranks and offices. Empress Dowager Ling allowed it. Cheng memorialized, "I have heard that the abuses of the three declining ages came from excessive punishments; the rise of the Fire Virtue rested on the Three Articles of law. Thus Lao Dan says, "The more laws and commands are displayed, the more thieves and robbers there are"; again, "When government is exacting, the people are impoverished"; and again, "The net of Heaven is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing escapes." Thus, to seek the root of good order, nothing is better than reducing affairs and clearing the mind. In the past, Emperor Wen of Han decided only four hundred cases and nearly brought punishment to rest; this came from reducing affairs. When Xiao He and Cao Shen served as ministers, songs praised their pure, quiet, and consistent rule; this was rooted in clearing the mind. If we now seek the root, we should begin by reducing affairs, so that officials continue the spirit of Xiao and Cao and assist the sacred transformation. Then ruler and subjects will be at peace, far and near will trust each other, the offices will not grow negligent, and affairs will not go astray. How could it be right to disturb the teaching of the age with over-subtle laws, or to cook small fish with fussy hands? I privately consider that from the start of Jingming to the end of Yongping, officials inside and outside the court underwent three evaluations. Only at the start of Yanchang were promotions and demotions applied. Those of the fifth rank and above were brought into the court hall and personally judged by His Majesty; those of the sixth rank and below were decided by edict as a rule. Since Shizong's death, three great amnesties have been issued to wipe away old intentions and begin anew. To reopen and investigate matters from a previous reign now is, in my foolish view, impermissible. Moreover, the Department of State Affairs has its own function: receiving and issuing the pivotal business of government. In the past, Emperor Ming of Wei suddenly arrived at the Department gate; Chen Jiao remonstrated firmly, and the emperor withdrew in shame. If even the lord of ten thousand chariots, when he went somewhere improper, yielded to one word and turned back ashamed, how can the officials and offices be allowed to intrude on one another? Thus Chen Ping did not know the accounts of coin and grain, and Bing Ji did not ask about the dead man lying by the road. Their age considered this good understanding of government, and later generations praised it. Each man should keep to his own office, think without overstepping his position, keep himself pure to encourage the age, and be quiet and reverent to achieve integrity. Moreover, the censorate's role is to act on reports. False claims of merit and reckless evaluations each have their proper offices. If rumors arise in one place, seize that one register and examine truth and falsehood; if discrepancies appear, the fraud will reveal itself. Then punish by statute, and who will not submit? How can one move the files of an entire department, seize the registers of the whole empire, search through two decades of affairs, and pursue every fault of a former reign? If faults are sought this way, who could bear the guilt? This is truly something the sacred court should treat with the greatest caution." Empress Dowager Ling accepted this, and the matter was stopped. Later he was promoted to Minister over the Masses, while remaining Palace Attendant and Director of the Department of State Affairs as before. Cheng also memorialized, "I humbly recall that Emperor Xuanwu, Shizong, commissioned generals and granted banners; Sui and Lu bowed their heads, and through his strategy the Huai and Han submitted of themselves. He saved resources and exhausted his mind, intending to clear the six directions. Thus he continued military achievement and cultivated civil rule, and the dynasty grew stronger generation after generation. Your Majesty lives in a time like the tranquil rule of King Kang of Zhou; how could you rest in silent ease? Yet to take what lies outside, one must first strengthen what lies within; to plan against others, one must first prepare oneself. Although Xiao Yan oppresses his people cruelly, he never stops coveting our lands. If he finds us empty and exhausted, our soldiers and people worn down, then the aged rebel Yan, his ambition still swelling, will try to spread his venom. If we do not plan for this, I fear we will suffer. Your Majesty occupies the throne at a fine young age, and your sacred virtue is just ascending; the Empress Dowager directs the machinery of state, diligent and watchful day and night. If you keep the state's burden in mind and resent that carriage tracks and writing are not yet unified; if you advance worthies, select the able, and treat official appointments as weighty; if you reward loyalty and purity and recognize men fit to nurture the people; if you strengthen the use of arms and store up bear-and-tiger warriors; if you cherish time, despise mere wealth, treat treasures lightly, and value grain; then in seven or eight years Your Majesty's strategy will be vigorous, the imperial princes' virtue and capacity will be mature, the generals and ministers will not yet have lost their strength, I will still be fit for the ranks, the armored troops will have stored up their sharpness, and the famous bows of Yan and horses of Ji will again be plentiful; moreover Xiao Yan's evil will have ripened into disaster, his power cannot last, his sons and brothers are dark and perverse, and their rebellious rifts are already clear. The signs of chaos and ruin are plainly visible. The signs point to annexing the weak; Heaven's gift is not far away, and the moment for great unity should be met with stored preparations. In the past, the Han emperor forced himself through illness to destroy Ying Bu; our High Emperor lay ill, yet personally eliminated Xianda. How could rulers of ten thousand chariots forget comfort and security? They acted because names were violated and order disturbed, leaving no alternative. Now we should emulate the far-reaching plans of those two emperors and make solemn pacification our great task. Yet in recent years, hard campaigns against raiders in east and west have followed one another. Though they were soon eliminated, they greatly damaged our resources and strength. Hungry people scatter and cannot be secured; revenues do not grow, while expenses multiply. If we do not spare labor to please the people and build resources to await the enemy, I will continue to worry day and night, fearful and uneasy. The Changes says, "How does one hold position? By benevolence. How does one gather people? By wealth." Thus wealth is not born without Heaven, does not grow without Earth, does not mature without the seasons, and does not gather without people. Producing and gathering it is this difficult; gathering people and holding position are this weighty. How can one fail to consider the path of rise and decline? In antiquity, labor service imposed on the people did not exceed three days a year; the grain of the strong was used, and the wisdom of the old was employed. Although this is a rule for an age of great peace and cannot be followed all at once, should we not be warned against harming the people and wasting wealth? Now the walls and battlements are already repaired, and the stables and storehouses stand in lofty rows. Although some offices, temples, schools, and halls are not yet complete, the government offices are generally sufficient for work and rest, and the temples and spirit towers suffice for worship and teaching. Only the Mingtang and Biyong are major matters of state ritual. When the Minister over the Masses' troops arrive next winter, I ask that other works be reduced or dismantled, effort focused on these projects, and every effort made to complete them early. Funds for Guangji, repeated almsgiving, merchant payments, and market exchanges, and all construction not urgently needed for imperial supply or military equipment, should be modestly reduced. This will build stores, prevent irregular losses to the treasuries, and preserve the people's strength. Gui's virtue shone because he ate from earthen vessels; Yu's achievement flourished though he slept in a humble room. Zhangtai was splendid and Chu weakened; Epang was grand and Qin's wealth ran dry. The causes of survival and destruction are plain to see. I hope you will reflect on the former kings' achievement in unifying all, store strength and gather wealth, and wait for the right moment." Empress Dowager Ling was eager for construction. In the capital she built Buddhist temples such as Yongning and Taishanggong at considerable cost; in the outer provinces, each built five-tiered stupas. She also repeatedly held universal vegetarian assemblies, where gifts often ran into the tens of thousands. The people were exhausted by earthwork and carpentry, and the price of gold and silver soared. Officials' labor resources were seized, the treasuries drained, and special gifts to attendants reached several thousand each day. This was why Cheng submitted the memorial. Although she ultimately did not follow it, she always replied graciously and treated him with courtesy. In affairs of government, great or small, he was always brought in to take part in decisions. Cheng devoted himself fully to correction and support. Whenever something was harmful to the people, he remonstrated; even when not heeded, he persisted earnestly. Those inside and outside the court all respected and feared him. He died in Shengui year 2 at the age of fifty-three. For funeral gifts he received twelve hundred bolts of cloth, six hundred thousand cash, and four hundred jin of wax; he was given an Eastern Garden Wenming coffin, one set of court robes, and one suit of clothing; the Grand Herald oversaw the funeral, and an edict ordered the officials to attend; he was posthumously granted Acting Yellow Axe, Bearer of the Staff, Commander of all military affairs inside and outside the court, Grand Tutor, and concurrently Grand Commandant; special rites were added, including the full Nine Bestowments, following the precedent of Sima You, Grand Marshal of Jin and Prince of Qi; His posthumous title was Prince Wenxuan. At Cheng's burial, the mourning regalia were extremely grand. Empress Dowager Ling personally escorted him beyond the suburbs, stopped her carriage, and wept bitterly, moving all those around her. More than a thousand officials attended, and all sighed and wept. At the time this was considered the height of mourning and honor.
4
第四子獻，襲。
The fourth son, Xian, inherited.
5
彝，字子倫，繼室馮氏所生，頗有父風。 拜通直散騎常侍。 及元叉專權，而彝耻於託附，故不得顯職。 莊帝初，河陰遇害，贈車騎將軍、儀同三司、青州刺史。 諡曰文。 子度世，襲。 武定中，金紫光祿大夫。
Yi, courtesy name Zilun, was born to Cheng's second wife Lady Feng and had much of his father's manner. He was appointed Regular Cavalier Attendant for Unrestricted Attendance. When Yuan Cha monopolized power, Yi was ashamed to attach himself to him and therefore did not obtain prominent office. At the start of Emperor Zhuang's reign, he was killed at Heyin and posthumously granted General of Chariots and Cavalry, Equal in Honor to the Three Excellencies, and Inspector of Qingzhou. His posthumous title was Wen. His son Dushi succeeded. In the Wuding era, he served as Gold and Purple Guanglu Grandee.
6
齊受禪，爵例降。 彝兄順，字子和。 九歲師事樂安陳豐，初書王羲之小學篇數千言，晝夜誦之，旬有五日，一皆通徹。 豐奇之，白澄曰：「豐十五從師，迄于白首，耳目所經，未見此比，江夏黃童，不得無雙也。」 澄笑曰：「藍田生玉，何容不爾。」 十六，通杜氏春秋，恒集門生，討論同異。 于時四方無事，國富民康，豪貴子弟，率以朋遊為樂，而順下帷讀書，篤志愛古。 性謇諤，淡於榮利，好飲酒，解鼓琴，能長吟永歎，吒詠虛室。 世宗時，上魏頌，文多不載。 起家為給事中。 時尚書令高肇，帝舅權重，天下人士，望塵拜伏。 順曾懷刺詣肇門，門者以其年少，答云「在坐大有貴客」，不肯為通。 順叱之曰：「任城王兒，可是賤也！」 及見，直往登牀，捧手抗禮，王公先達，莫不怪慴，而順辭吐傲然，若無所覩。 肇謂眾賓曰：「此兒豪氣尚爾，況其父乎！」 及出，肇加敬送之。 澄聞之，大怒，杖之數十。 後超轉中書侍郎，俄遷太常少卿。 以父憂去職，哭泣嘔血，身自負土。 時年二十五，便有白髮，免喪抽去，不復更生，世人以為孝思所致。 尋除給事黃門侍郎。 時領軍元叉威勢尤盛，凡有遷授，莫不造門謝謁。 順拜表而已，曾不詣叉。 叉謂順曰：「卿何謂聊不見我？」 順正色曰：「天子富於春秋，委政宗輔，叔父宜以至公為心，舉士報國，如何賣恩，責人私謝，豈所望也！」 至於朝論得失，順常鯁言正議，曾不阿旨，由此見憚。 出除平北將軍、恒州刺史。
