順謂叉曰：「北鎮紛紜，方為國梗，桑乾舊都，根本所繫，請假都督，為國捍屏。」 叉心疑難，不欲授以兵官，謂順曰：「此朝廷之事，非我所裁。」 順曰：「叔父既握國柄，殺生由己，自言天之歷數應在我躬，何得復有朝廷也！」 叉彌忿憚之。 轉為安東將軍、齊州刺史。 順自負有才，不得居內，每懷鬱怏，形於言色，遂縱酒歡娛，不親政事。 叉解領軍，徵為給事黃門侍郎。 親友郊迎，賀其得入。 順曰：「不患不入，正恐入而復出耳。」 俄兼殿中尚書，轉侍中。 初，中山王熙起兵討元叉，不果而誅，及靈太后反政，方得改葬。 順侍坐西遊園，因奏太后曰：「臣昨往看中山家葬，非唯宗親哀其冤酷，行路士女，見其一家七喪，皆為澘然，莫不酸泣。」 叉妻時在太后側，順指之曰：「陛下奈何以一妹之故，不伏元叉之罪，使天下懷冤！」 太后默然不語。 就德興反於營州，使尚書盧同往討之，大敗而返。 屬侍中穆紹與順侍坐，因論同之罪。 同先有近宅借紹，紹頗欲為言。 順勃然曰：「盧同終將無罪！」 太后曰：「何得如侍中之言？」 順曰：「同有好宅與要勢侍中，豈慮罪也。」 紹慚，不敢復言。 靈太后頗事妝飾，數出遊幸。 順面諍曰：「禮，婦人夫喪，自稱未亡人，首去珠玉，衣不被綵。 陛下母臨天下，年垂不惑，過甚修飾，何以示後世？」 靈太后慚而不出。 還入宮，責順曰：「千里相徵，豈欲眾中見辱也！」 順曰：「陛下盛服炫容，不畏天下所笑，何耻臣之一言乎？」 初，城陽王徽慕順才名，偏相結納。 而廣陽王淵姦徽妻于氏，大為嫌隙。 及淵自定州被徵，入為吏部尚書，兼中領軍。 順為詔書，辭頗優美。 徽疑順為淵左右，由是與徐紇間順於靈太后，出順為護軍將軍、太常卿。 順奉辭於西遊園，徽紇侍側，順指之謂靈太后曰：「此人魏之宰嚭，魏國不滅，終不死亡。」 紇脅肩而出。 順遂抗聲叱之曰：「爾刀筆小人，正堪為几案之吏，寧應忝茲執戟，虧我彝倫！」 遂振衣而起。 靈太后默而不言。 時追論順父顧託之功，增任城王彝邑二千戶，又析彝邑五百戶以封順，為東阿縣開國公。 順疾徽等間之，遂為蠅賦曰：「余以仲秋休沐，端坐衡門，寄想琴書，託情紙翰，而蒼蠅小蟲，往來牀几，疾其變白，聊為賦云：遐哉大道，廓矣洪氛。 肇立秋夏，爰啟冬春。 既含育於萬性，又芻狗而不仁。 隨因緣以授體，齊美惡而無分。 生茲穢類，靡益於人。 名備羣品，聲損眾倫。 欹脛纖翼，紫首蒼身。 飛不能迥，聲若遠聞。 點緇成素，變白為黑。 寡愛蘭芳，偏貪穢食。 集桓公之屍，居平叔之側。 亂鷄鳴之響，毀皇宮之飾。 習習戶庭，營營榛棘。 反覆往還，譬彼讒賊。 膚受既通，譖潤罔極。 緝緝幡幡，交亂四國。 於是妖姬進，邪士來，聖賢擁，忠孝摧。 周昌拘於牖里，天乙囚於夏臺。 伯奇為之痛結，申生為之蒙災。 鴟鴞悲其室，採葛懼其懷。 小弁隕其涕，靈均表其哀。 自古明哲猶如此，何況中庸與凡才。 若夫天生地養，各有所親。 獸必依地，鳥亦憑雲。 或來儀以呈祉，或自擾而見文。 或負圖而歸德，或銜書以告真。 或夭胎而奉味，或殘軀以獻珍。 或主皮而興禮，或牢豢以供神。 雖死生之異質，俱有益於國人。 非如蒼蠅之無用，唯構亂於蒸民。」 遂屬疾在家，杜絕慶弔。 後除吏部尚書，兼右僕射。 及上省，登階向榻，見榻甚故，問都令史徐仵起。 仵起曰：「此榻曾經先王坐。」 順即哽塞，涕泗交流，久而不能言，遂令換之。 時三公曹令史朱暉，素事錄尚書、高陽王雍，雍欲以為廷尉評，頻請託順，順不為用。 雍遂下命用之，順投之於地。 雍聞之，大怒，昧爽坐都廳，召尚書及丞郎畢集，欲待順至，於眾挫之。 順日高方至，雍攘袂撫几而言曰：「身，天子之子，天子之弟，天子之叔，天子之相，四海之內，親尊莫二，元順何人，以身成命，投棄於地！」 順鬚鬢俱張，仰面看屋，憤氣奔涌，長歔而不言。 久之，搖一白羽扇，徐而謂雍曰：「高祖遷宅中土，創定九流，官方清濁，軌儀萬古。 而朱暉小子，身為省吏，何合為廷尉清官！ 殿下既先皇同氣，宜遵成旨，自有短垣而復踰之也。」 雍曰：「身為丞相、錄尚書，如何不得用一人為官？」 順曰：「庖人雖不治庖，尸祝不得越樽俎而代之。 未聞有別旨，令殿下參選事。」 順又厲聲曰：「殿下必如是，順當依事奏聞！」 雍遂笑而言曰：「豈可以朱暉小人，便相忿恨。」 遂起，呼順入室，與之極飲。 順之亢毅不撓，皆此類也。 後除征南將軍、右光祿大夫，轉兼左僕射。 爾朱榮之奉莊帝，召百官悉至河陰，素聞順數諫諍，惜其亮直，謂朱瑞曰：「可語元僕射，但在省，不須來。」 順不達其旨，聞害衣冠，遂便出走，為陵戶鮮于康奴所害。 家徒四壁，無物斂屍，止有書數千卷而已。 門下通事令史王才達裂裳覆之。 莊帝還宮，遣黃門侍郎山偉巡喻京邑。 偉臨順喪，悲慟無已。 既還，莊帝怪而問曰：「黃門何為聲散？」 偉以狀對。 莊帝敕侍中元祉曰：「宗室喪亡非一，不可周贍。 元僕射清苦之節，死乃益彰，特贈絹百匹，餘不得例。」 贈驃騎大將軍、尚書令、司徒公、定州刺史，諡曰文烈。 順撰帝錄二十卷，詩賦表頌數十篇，今多亡失。 長子朗，時年十七。 枕戈潛伏積年，乃手刃康奴，以首祭於順墓，然後詣闕請罪。 朝廷嘉而不問。 朗涉歷書記，為司徒屬。 天平中，為奴所害。 贈都督瀛冀二州諸軍事、□□將軍、尚書右僕射、冀州刺史。 順弟淑，淑弟悲，並早卒。 悲弟紀，字子綱。 永熙中，給事黃門侍郎。 隨出帝，沒於關中。 澄弟嵩，字道岳。 高祖時，自中大夫遷員外常侍，轉步兵校尉。 大司馬、安定王休薨，未及卒哭，嵩便遊田。 高祖聞而大怒，詔曰：「嵩不能克己復禮，企心典憲，大司馬薨殂甫爾，便以鷹鷂自娛。 有如父之痛，無猶子之情，捐心棄禮，何其太速！ 便可免官。」 後從平沔北，累有戰功，除左中郎將，兼武衞將軍。 高祖南伐，蕭寶卷將陳顯達率眾拒戰。 嵩身備三仗，免冑直前，將士從之，顯達奔潰，斬獲萬計。 嵩於爾日勇冠三軍。 高祖大悅而言曰：「任城康王大有褔德，文武頓出其門。」 以功賜爵高平縣侯，賚帛二千五百匹。 初，高祖之發洛也，馮皇后以罪幽於宮內。 既平顯達，回次穀唐原，高祖疾甚，將賜后死，曰：「使人不易可得。」 顧謂任城王澄曰：「任城必不負我，嵩亦當不負任城，可使嵩也。」 於是引嵩入內，親詔遣之。 世宗即位，以武衞將軍兼侍中，出為平南將軍、荊州刺史。 嵩表曰：「蕭寶卷骨肉相殘，忠良先戮，臣下囂然，莫不離背，君臣攜貳，干戈日尋。 流聞寶卷雍州刺史蕭衍兄懿於建業阻兵，與寶卷相持，荊郢二州刺史並是寶卷之弟，必有圖衍之志。 臣若遣書相聞，迎其本謀，冀獲同心，并力除衍。 平衍之後，彼必旋師赴救丹陽，當不能復經營疆陲，全固襄沔。 臣之軍威已得臨據，則沔南之地可一舉而收。 緣漢曜兵，示以威德，思歸有道者則引而納之，受疑告危者則援而接之。 總兵竚銳，觀釁伺隙，若其零落之形已彰，怠懈之勢已著，便可順流摧鋒，長驅席卷。」 詔曰：「所陳嘉謀，深是良計。 如當機形可進，任將軍裁之。」 既而蕭衍尋克建業，乃止。 除平北將軍、恒州刺史。 轉平東將軍、徐州刺史。 又轉安南將軍、揚州刺史。 蕭衍湘州刺史楊公則率眾二萬，屯軍洛口，姜慶真領卒五千，據於首陂，又遣其左軍將軍騫小眼，軍主何天祚、張俊興等率眾七千，攻圍陸城，嵩乃遣統軍封邁、王會等步騎八千討之。 邁達陸城，賊皆夜遁，追擊破之，斬獲數千，公則、慶真退還馬頭。 衍徐州刺史昌義之屯據高皇，遣三軍潛寇陰陵，以淮水淺竭，不通船艦，屯於馬頭。 衍將田道龍、何景先等領卒三千已至衡山，規寇陸城。 寇並充逼。 嵩遣兼統軍李叔仁等援合肥、小峴、楊石，頻戰破之。 衍征虜將軍趙草屯於黃口，嵩遣軍司趙熾等往討之，先遣統軍安伯醜潛師夜渡，伏兵下蔡。 草率卒四千，逆來拒戰，伯醜與下蔡戍主王虎等前後夾擊，大敗之，俘斬溺死四千餘人。 統軍李叔仁等夜襲硤石之賊，又破之。 衍將姜慶真專據肥汭，冠軍將軍曹天寶屯於鷄口，軍主尹明世屯東硤石。 嵩遣別將羊引次于淮西，去賊營十里，司馬趙熾率兵一萬為表裏聲勢。 眾軍既會，分擊賊之四壘。 四壘之賊，戰敗奔走，斬獲數千，溺死萬數。 統軍牛敬賓攻硤石，明世宵遁。 慶真合餘燼浮淮下，下蔡戍主王略截流擊之，俘斬太半。 於是威名大振。 後為蒼頭李太伯等同謀害嵩，并妻穆氏及子世賢。 世宗為嵩舉哀於東堂，賻絹一千匹，贈車騎將軍、領軍，諡曰剛侯。 第二子世儁，頗有幹用，而無行業。 襲爵，除給事中、東宮舍人。 伯父澄表求轉階授之，於是除員外散騎常侍。 肅宗時，追論嵩勳，封世儁衞縣開國男，食邑二百戶。 遷冠軍將軍、宗正少卿，又為散騎常侍、安南將軍、武衞將軍、河南尹。 尋除鎮東將軍、青州刺史，轉征東將軍，加散騎常侍。 邢杲之亂，圍逼州城，世儁憑城拒守，遂得保全。 孝莊時，除衞將軍、吏部尚書。 爾朱兆寇京師，詔世儁以本官為都督，防守河橋。 及兆至河，世儁初無拒守意，便隔岸遙拜，時論疾之。 前廢帝世，為驃騎將軍，仍加尚書，尤為爾朱世隆所昵。 出帝初，加儀同三司，改封武陽縣開國子，食邑五百戶。 世儁居選曹，不能厲心，多所受納，為中尉彈糾，坐免官。 尋復本職。 孝靜初，加侍中、尚書右僕射，遷尚書令。 世儁輕薄，好去就，詔送晉陽。 興和中，薨。 贈侍中、都督冀定瀛殷四州諸軍事、驃騎大將軍、太傅、定州刺史，尚書令、開國公如故，諡曰躁戾。 子景遠襲，散騎侍郎。 世賢弟世哲，武定中，吏部郎。 嵩弟贍，字道周。 高祖時，自□大夫稍遷宗正少卿、龍驤將軍、光州刺史、散騎常侍、左將軍，遷平東將軍、兗州刺史。 頗愛書史，而貪暴好殺。 澄深恥忿之，絕其往來。 有四子。 長子遠，尚書郎。 史臣曰：顯祖之將禪讓，可謂國之大節。 康王毅然庭諍，德音孔昭，一言興邦，其斯之謂歟？ 文宣貞固俊遠，鬱為宗傑，身因累朝，寧濟夷險，既社稷是任，其梁棟之望也。 順謇諤俶儻，有汲黯之風，不用於時，橫招非命，惜矣。 嵩有行陳之氣，儁則裂冠之徒歟？
After Qi took the throne, enfeoffments were lowered by precedent. Yi's elder brother Shun was styled Zihe. At nine, he studied with Chen Feng of Le'an. He first copied several thousand words of Wang Xizhi's Elementary Primer, reciting it day and night, and in fifteen days he had mastered it all. Feng marveled and told Cheng, "I have studied with teachers from the age of fifteen to white-haired old age, and never in all I have seen or heard have I met his equal. The yellow-haired prodigy of Jiangxia cannot be peerless after all." Cheng smiled. "Lantian produces jade; how could it be otherwise?" At sixteen he mastered Master Du's Spring and Autumn and often gathered students to debate points of agreement and difference. At the time the frontiers were quiet, the state was rich, and the people were at peace. The sons of the powerful generally amused themselves with companions, but Shun shut himself behind the curtain to read, devoted to antiquity. He was naturally blunt, indifferent to honor and profit, fond of wine, and skilled at the zither; he could chant at length, sigh deeply, and sing out in an empty room. During Shizong's reign he submitted a Eulogy of Wei, though much of the text is not preserved. He began his career as Supervising Attendant. At the time Gao Zhao, Director of the Department and the emperor's maternal uncle, held immense power; men throughout the realm bowed before even the dust of his carriage. Shun once brought a calling card to Zhao's gate. Seeing his youth, the gatekeeper answered, "There are many great guests seated inside," and refused to announce him. Shun scolded him: "Can the son of the Prince of Rencheng be someone base?" When admitted, he went straight to the couch, mounted it, clasped his hands, and greeted Zhao as an equal. Princes, dukes, and elder worthies were all startled and awed, while Shun spoke proudly as if no one else were there. Zhao told his guests, "If the boy's spirit is already like this, how much more his father!" When Shun left, Zhao treated him with added respect and saw him off. When Cheng heard of this, he was furious and had him caned several dozen strokes. Later he was promoted out of turn to Secretariat Attendant, and soon advanced to Junior Chamberlain for Ceremonials. He left office to mourn his father, wept until he vomited blood, and carried earth for the grave himself. He was twenty-five at the time, yet already had white hair. After mourning ended he plucked it out, and it never grew back; people believed this came from filial grief. Soon he was appointed Attendant of the Yellow Gate. At the time Yuan Cha, Commander of the Guards, was extremely powerful. Whenever anyone received a transfer or appointment, he went to Yuan Cha's gate to give thanks. Shun merely submitted a memorial of thanks and never called on Yuan Cha. Yuan Cha said to Shun, "Why have you not come to see me at all?" Shun answered sternly, "The Son of Heaven is young and has entrusted government to clan ministers. Uncle should act with perfect fairness, raise worthy men, and serve the state. How can you sell favors and demand private thanks? This is not what one expects." In court debates over right and wrong, Shun always spoke bluntly and argued uprightly, never bending to anyone's wishes; for this he was feared. He was sent out as General Who Pacifies the North and Inspector of Hengzhou. Shun told Yuan Cha, "The northern garrisons are in turmoil and threaten the state. Sanggan and the old capital are bound to our foundation. Give me temporary command, and I will serve as the state's shield." Yuan Cha was suspicious and reluctant to give him a military post, so he said, "This is a court matter, not mine to decide." Shun said, "Uncle holds state power, and life and death come from you. You yourself say Heaven's mandate should rest in your own person; how can there still be a court?" Yuan Cha grew even angrier and more afraid of him. Shun was transferred to General Who Pacifies the East and Inspector of Qizhou. Confident in his talent and unable to remain at court, Shun nursed resentment that showed in his face and speech. He then gave himself over to wine and amusement and neglected government. When Yuan Cha was relieved of command of the Guards, Shun was summoned as Attendant of the Yellow Gate. Relatives and friends met him in the suburbs and congratulated him on returning to court. Shun said, "I am not worried about failing to enter; I only fear entering and then being sent out again." Soon he concurrently served as Minister of the Palace and was then transferred to Palace Attendant. Earlier, Xi, Prince of Zhongshan, had raised troops against Yuan Cha, failed, and been executed. Only after Empress Dowager Ling resumed power was he allowed reburial. While sitting in attendance in the Western Tour Garden, Shun said to the Empress Dowager, "Yesterday I went to see the burial of the Zhongshan household. Not only did the imperial kin mourn their cruel wrong; travelers, men and women alike, saw seven dead from one family and all wept bitterly." Yuan Cha's wife was beside the Empress Dowager at the time. Shun pointed to her and said, "How can Your Majesty, for the sake of one sister, fail to punish Yuan Cha's crime and leave the whole realm nursing injustice?" The Empress Dowager was silent. When Jiu Dexing rebelled in Yingzhou, Lu Tong of the Department was sent against him but returned after a major defeat. Palace Attendant Mu Shao happened to be sitting in attendance with Shun, and they discussed Lu Tong's offense. Lu Tong had earlier lent Shao a nearby residence, and Shao wanted to speak for him. Shun suddenly said, "Lu Tong will end up without guilt!" The Empress Dowager said, "How can it be as the Palace Attendant says?" Shun replied, "Tong has a fine house to give a powerful Palace Attendant. Why should he worry about guilt?" Shao was ashamed and did not dare speak again. Empress Dowager Ling was much occupied with adornment and often went out on excursions. Shun remonstrated with her directly: "According to ritual, when a woman loses her husband she calls herself the one not yet dead, removes pearls and jade from her hair, and does not wear colored clothing. Your Majesty rules the realm as mother and is nearly forty, yet you adorn yourself excessively. What example does this show later generations?" Empress Dowager Ling was ashamed and stopped going out. When she returned to the palace, she rebuked Shun: "I summoned you from a thousand li away; did you intend to shame me in public?" Shun replied, "Your Majesty dresses splendidly and displays your beauty without fearing the laughter of the realm. Why be ashamed of one word from me?" Earlier, Hui, Prince of Chengyang, admired Shun's talent and reputation and made special efforts to befriend him. But Yuan, Prince of Guangyang, had an affair with Hui's wife Lady Yu, creating a deep rift. When Yuan was summoned from Dingzhou to serve as Minister of Personnel and concurrently Central Commander of the Guards, Shun drafted the edict for him in notably elegant language. Hui suspected Shun of favoring Yuan, so he and Xu He slandered Shun to Empress Dowager Ling. Shun was sent out as General Who Protects the Army and Chamberlain for Ceremonials. Shun took leave in the Western Tour Garden while Hui and Xu He stood at the side. Pointing at Xu He, he said to Empress Dowager Ling, "This man is Wei's Zai Pi. Unless Wei is destroyed, he will never die." Xu He went out with his shoulders hunched. Shun then shouted after him, "You petty clerk with knife and brush are fit only for desk work. How can you presume to hold a halberd here and disgrace our proper order!" He shook out his robe and rose. Empress Dowager Ling said nothing. At the time the court was reviewing the merit of Shun's father in the imperial entrustment. Yi, Prince of Rencheng, received two thousand additional households, and five hundred households were carved from Yi's fief to enfeoff Shun as Founding Duke of Dong'e County. Shun hated Hui and the others for slandering him, and so he wrote a Rhapsody on Flies: "In mid-autumn, resting from office, I sat quietly at my humble gate, my thoughts on zither and books and my feelings entrusted to paper and brush. But tiny bluebottle flies came and went over bed and table. Hating how they transform white, I have made this rhapsody: Vast is the great Way, broad the primal vapor. It first set autumn and summer in place, then opened winter and spring. It contains and nurtures all natures, yet like straw dogs it is not benevolent. Following conditions, it grants bodies, making no distinction between fair and foul. Thus this filthy kind is born, bringing no benefit to people. Its name is counted among living things, but its buzzing harms the order of all beings. Crooked legs, slender wings, purple heads, blue bodies. It cannot fly far, yet its noise seems to carry into the distance. It spots black onto white and turns white into black. It cares little for orchid fragrance and craves filthy food. It gathered on Duke Huan's corpse and lingered at Pingshu's side. It confused the sound of the cockcrow and defiled the ornaments of the imperial palace. Fluttering through doors and courtyards, buzzing among thorns and brambles. Back and forth it comes and goes, like slanderous traitors. Once slander penetrates the skin, its soaking accusations know no limit. Whispering and fluttering, they throw the four quarters into disorder. Then seductive women advance, wicked men arrive, sages and worthies are blocked, and the loyal and filial are crushed. Zhou Chang was confined at Youli, and Tianyi imprisoned at Xiatai. Boqi was bound in grief because of them, and Shensheng was overtaken by disaster because of them. The Owl lamented its ruined house, and Gathering Kudzu feared what lay in the heart. Xiaobian shed tears, and Lingjun made his sorrow known. Even the enlightened and wise of antiquity suffered so; how much more men of middling or ordinary talent? As for the beings Heaven gives birth to and Earth nourishes, each has its proper affinities. Beasts rely on the earth, and birds depend on the clouds. Some come in stately display to present blessings; some are domesticated and display patterned beauty. Some bear diagrams and return to virtue; some carry writings in their mouths to reveal the true. Some are taken before birth to provide flavor; some, with damaged bodies, offer delicacies. Some, as hides, give rise to ritual; some, as sacrificial animals, serve the spirits. Though they differ as living and dead, all benefit the people of the state. They are not like the bluebottle fly, useless and only sowing disorder among the people." He then fell ill at home and refused all visits of congratulation or condolence. Later he was appointed Minister of Personnel and concurrently Right Vice Director. When he went up to the Department and approached the couch, he saw that it was very old and asked Chief Clerk Xu Wuqi about it. Wuqi said, "The former prince once sat on this couch." Shun immediately choked up, tears streaming down; for a long while he could not speak, and then ordered the couch replaced. At the time Zhu Hui, a clerk in the Bureau of the Three Excellencies, had long served Yuan Yong, Prince of Gaoyang and Recording Director of the Department. Yong wanted to make him an Evaluator in the Court of Justice and repeatedly pressed Shun, but Shun refused to use him. Yuan Yong then issued an order appointing him, and Shun threw it on the ground. When Yong heard, he was furious. At dawn he sat in the metropolitan hall and summoned all the Ministers, Aides, and Gentlemen, intending to humiliate Shun publicly when he arrived. Shun arrived only when the sun was high. Yong rolled up his sleeves, struck the table, and said, "I am the Son of Heaven's son, brother, uncle, and chief minister. Within the four seas no one is closer or more honored. Who is Yuan Shun, to take my completed order and throw it on the ground!" Shun's beard and temples bristled. He looked up at the rafters, anger surging, and gave a long sigh without speaking. After a long while, he waved a white feather fan and slowly said to Yong, "Gaozu moved the capital to the central lands and established the nine ranks; he distinguished pure and impure offices, setting a model for all ages. Zhu Hui is a petty man, a mere Department clerk. How is he fit for a pure office in the Court of Justice? Your Highness shares the late emperor's blood and should follow the established decree. Even a low wall is still a boundary; why overstep it again?" Yong said, "I am Chancellor and Recording Director of the Department. How can I not appoint one man to office?" Shun replied, "Even if the cook does not manage the kitchen, the invocator may not step beyond the vessels and stands to take his place. I have heard of no separate edict ordering Your Highness to take part in personnel selection." Shun then said sharply, "If Your Highness insists, I will memorialize the matter according to the facts!" Yong then laughed. "How could we become angry with one another over a petty man like Zhu Hui?" He rose, called Shun inside, and drank with him to the fullest. Shun's lofty firmness and refusal to bend were all of this sort. Later he was appointed General Who Conquers the South and Right Guanglu Grandee, then transferred to concurrently serve as Left Vice Director. When Erzhu Rong received Emperor Zhuang, he summoned all officials to Heyin. Having long heard that Shun often remonstrated and valuing his clear integrity, he told Zhu Rui, "Tell Vice Director Yuan to stay in the Department; he need not come." Shun did not understand the warning. Hearing that the officials were being slaughtered, he fled and was killed by Xianyu Kangnu, a tomb-household man. His house was bare, with nothing to shroud his body; it contained only several thousand scrolls of books. Wang Caida, Clerk for Communications under the Gate, tore his robe to cover the body. When Emperor Zhuang returned to the palace, he sent Yellow Gate Attendant Shan Wei to tour the capital and reassure it. Shan Wei visited Shun's mourning place and wept without stopping. When he returned, Emperor Zhuang was surprised and asked, "Why is the Yellow Gate attendant's voice hoarse?" Shan Wei told him what had happened. Emperor Zhuang instructed Palace Attendant Yuan Zhi, "Many members of the imperial clan have died, and we cannot provide fully for all of them. Vice Director Yuan's austere integrity shines even more in death. Grant him one hundred bolts of silk as a special gift; let this not become precedent for the others." He was posthumously granted Grand General of Agile Cavalry, Director of the Department of State Affairs, Minister over the Masses, and Inspector of Dingzhou, and was given the posthumous title Wenlie. Shun compiled Imperial Records in twenty fascicles and wrote several dozen poems, rhapsodies, memorials, and eulogies, most of which are now lost. His eldest son Lang was seventeen at the time. For years he slept on his spear and hid in secret. Then he killed Kangnu with his own hand, offered the head at Shun's tomb, and afterward went to the palace gate to confess. The court praised him and did not punish him. Lang was experienced in documents and records and served as an attendant to the Minister over the Masses. In the Tianping era, he was killed by a slave. He was posthumously granted Commander of all military affairs in Ying and Ji provinces, an unspecified generalship, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Inspector of Jizhou. Shun's younger brother Shu and Shu's younger brother Bei both died young. Bei's younger brother Ji was styled Zigang. In the Yongxi era he served as Attendant of the Yellow Gate. He followed the Emperor Who Went Out and died in Guanzhong. Cheng's younger brother Song was styled Daoyue. In Gaozu's time he moved from Palace Grandee to Regular Attendant Outside the Ranks, then became Infantry Commandant. When Xiu, Grand Marshal and Prince of Anding, died, Song went hunting before the mourning rites had even ended. When Gaozu heard, he was furious and issued an edict: "Song cannot master himself and return to ritual or set his mind on law and precedent. The Grand Marshal has only just died, and already he amuses himself with hawks and falcons. He should feel pain as for a father, yet he lacks even a nephew's feeling; he casts aside feeling and abandons ritual. How terribly hasty! He may be dismissed from office." Later he took part in pacifying the north of the Mian, repeatedly earned battle merit, and was appointed Left Gentleman General of the Center, concurrently General of the Martial Guard. When Gaozu campaigned south, Xiao Baojuan's general Chen Xianda led troops to resist him. Song armed himself with three weapons, removed his helmet, and advanced straight ahead. The officers and soldiers followed; Xianda's forces fled in collapse, and the dead and captured numbered in the tens of thousands. That day, Song's courage surpassed the whole army. Gaozu was delighted. "Prince Kang of Rencheng had great fortune and virtue; civil and martial talent have both burst from his household." For his merit he was granted the title Marquis of Gaoping County and awarded twenty-five hundred bolts of silk. Earlier, when Gaozu left Luoyang, Empress Feng had been confined inside the palace for an offense. After Xianda was defeated, Gaozu stopped on the return at Gutangyuan. Gravely ill, he was about to order the empress to die and said, "A suitable envoy is not easy to find." He turned to Cheng, Prince of Rencheng: "Rencheng will not fail me, and Song will not fail Rencheng. Send Song." Song was then brought inside, and Gaozu personally ordered him dispatched. When Shizong ascended the throne, Song served as General of the Martial Guard and concurrently Palace Attendant, then was sent out as General Who Pacifies the South and Inspector of Jingzhou. Song memorialized, "Xiao Baojuan slaughters his own kin and kills loyal men first. His ministers are in uproar and all are turning from him. Ruler and ministers are divided, and war grows daily. I have heard that Xiao Yi, elder brother of Xiao Yan, Baojuan's Inspector of Yongzhou, is holding troops at Jianye against Baojuan; the Inspectors of Jingzhou and Yingzhou are both Baojuan's younger brothers and surely plan to move against Yan. If I send letters and meet them in their own plans, we may act with one mind and combine forces to eliminate Yan. Once Yan is pacified, they will have to turn back to rescue Danyang and will no longer be able to manage the frontier or secure Xiang and Mian. If our army has already established a commanding position, the land south of the Mian can be taken in a single move. If we display troops along the Han and show both power and virtue, those who wish to return to the Way can be welcomed, and those in danger under suspicion can be rescued and received. With troops gathered and ready, we can watch for cracks and openings. Once their collapse is clear and their slackness plain, we can move with the current, break their front, drive deep, and sweep them up like a mat." The edict said, "The fine plan you present is truly sound strategy. If the moment and situation permit an advance, the General may decide." Soon afterward Xiao Yan captured Jianye, and the plan was dropped. Song was appointed General Who Pacifies the North and Inspector of Hengzhou. He was transferred to General Who Pacifies the East and Inspector of Xuzhou. He was later transferred again as General Who Pacifies the South and Inspector of Yangzhou. Yang Gongze, Xiao Yan's Inspector of Xiangzhou, led twenty thousand men to Luokou; Jiang Qingzhen led five thousand to Shoubei; and Yan sent Left Army General Qian Xiaoyan, with army commanders He Tianzuo, Zhang Junxing, and others, leading seven thousand men to besiege Lucheng. Song sent Feng Mai, Wang Hui, and other commanders with eight thousand infantry and cavalry against them. When Feng Mai reached Lucheng, the rebels fled by night. He pursued and defeated them, killing or capturing several thousand, while Gongze and Qingzhen retreated to Matou. Chang Yizhi, Yan's Inspector of Xuzhou, held Gaohuang and sent three armies in a secret raid on Yinling. Since the Huai was too shallow for boats to pass, he stationed at Matou. Yan's generals Tian Daolong, He Jingxian, and others led three thousand soldiers to Hengshan, planning to raid Lucheng. The raiders pressed in from all sides. Song sent acting Commander Li Shuren and others to reinforce Hefei, Xiaoxian, and Yangshi, repeatedly defeating the enemy in battle. Zhao Cao, Yan's General Who Conquers Caitiffs, was stationed at Huangkou. Song sent Army Marshal Zhao Chi and others to attack, first dispatching Commander An Bochou to cross secretly by night and set an ambush at Xiacai. Zhao Cao led four thousand men to meet them. An Bochou and Wang Hu, commander of Xiacai Garrison, struck from front and rear, badly defeated him, and captured, killed, or drowned more than four thousand men. Commander Li Shuren and others made a night attack on the rebels at Xiashi and defeated them as well. Yan's general Jiang Qingzhen held Feirui, Champion General Cao Tianbao was stationed at Jikou, and army commander Yin Mingshi at Eastern Xiashi. Song sent the separate general Yang Yin to camp at Huaixi, ten li from the rebel camp, while Marshal Zhao Chi led ten thousand troops to create pressure from inside and outside. When the armies had assembled, they split up and attacked the rebels' four forts. The rebels in the four forts were defeated and fled; several thousand were killed or captured, and tens of thousands drowned. Commander Niu Jingbin attacked Xiashi, and Yin Mingshi fled by night. Jiang Qingzhen gathered the remnants and moved down the Huai; Wang Lue, commander of Xiacai Garrison, intercepted him on the river and captured or killed more than half. Thereafter Song's reputation for military power greatly flourished. Later Li Taibo and other cangtou retainers conspired to murder Song, together with his wife Lady Mu and his son Shixian. Shizong held mourning for Song in the Eastern Hall, granted one thousand bolts of silk for the funeral, posthumously awarded him General of Chariots and Cavalry and Commander of the Guards, and gave him the posthumous title Marquis Gang. His second son Shijun had some practical ability but no moral conduct. He inherited the title and was appointed Supervising Attendant and Household Gentleman of the Eastern Palace. His uncle Cheng memorialized asking that a rank be transferred to him, and Shijun was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Outside the Ranks. In Suzong's reign, Song's merits were reviewed, and Shijun was enfeoffed as Founding Baron of Wei County with two hundred households. He rose to Champion General and Junior Chamberlain for the Imperial Clan, then served as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Who Pacifies the South, General of the Martial Guard, and Governor of Henan. Soon he was appointed General Who Guards the East and Inspector of Qingzhou, then transferred to General Who Conquers the East with the added title Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary. During Xing Gao's rebellion, the provincial city was surrounded and pressed hard. Shijun held the walls and defended it, preserving the city intact. In Emperor Xiaozhuang's reign, he was appointed General of the Guard and Minister of Personnel. When Erzhu Zhao raided the capital, an edict kept Shijun in his current office and made him Commander-in-Chief for the defense of Heqiao. When Zhao reached the river, Shijun had no intention of resisting. He immediately bowed from across the bank, and public opinion despised him. Under the Former Deposed Emperor, he was General of Agile Cavalry with the added title Minister of State Affairs, and he was especially close to Erzhu Shilong. At the start of the Emperor Who Went Out's reign, he was given Equal in Honor to the Three Excellencies and re-enfeoffed as Founding Viscount of Wuyang County with five hundred households. While Shijun served in the selections bureau, he failed to discipline himself and accepted many gifts. The Censor-in-Chief impeached him, and he was dismissed. Soon he was restored to his former office. At the start of Emperor Xiaojing's reign, he was made Palace Attendant and Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, then promoted to Director of the Department. Shijun was frivolous and fond of shifting allegiance, so an edict sent him to Jinyang. He died in the Xinghe era. He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant, Commander of all military affairs in Ji, Ding, Ying, and Yin provinces, Grand General of Agile Cavalry, Grand Tutor, and Inspector of Dingzhou, while retaining Director of the Department of State Affairs and Founding Duke as before. His posthumous title was Zaoli. His son Jingyuan succeeded and served as Cavalier Attendant. Shixian's younger brother Shizhe served in the Wuding era as Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel. Song's younger brother Zhan was styled Daozhou. In Gaozu's time, from a Grandee title with one missing character, he gradually rose to Junior Chamberlain for the Imperial Clan, Longxiang General, Inspector of Guangzhou, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and General of the Left, then was promoted to General Who Pacifies the East and Inspector of Yanzhou. He had some love for books and histories, but was greedy, violent, and fond of killing. Cheng was deeply ashamed and angered by him and broke off all contact. He had four sons. The eldest son, Yuan, was a Gentleman of the Department of State Affairs. The historian says: When Xianzu was about to abdicate, it was a great test of the state. Prince Kang remonstrated firmly in court, his virtuous words shining clearly; one word raised the state. Is this not the phrase made real? Wenxuan was upright, firm, outstanding, and far-seeing, a flourishing hero of the imperial clan. Serving through successive reigns, calm in ease and danger, he bore responsibility for the state and was the hope of its beams and pillars. Shun was blunt and free-spirited, with the air of Ji An. Unused by his time, he wrongly met an untimely death. A pity! Song had the spirit of the battle line; Jun was surely a cap-tearing sort of man, was he not?
